q: Unsure of my duty or what to do
Afraid of failure, attached to results
h: A boy who went to Death's house and asked what happens after we die.
Death, the lord of the departed, who becomes Nachiketa's teacher.
Nachiketa's father, who gave away worn-out cows at a sacrifice.
A boy who did not know his father, told the truth, and became a great teacher.
Satyakama's mother, who told her son the plain truth about his birth.
The teacher who accepted Satyakama because he told the truth.
Satyakama's student, taught by the sacred fires when his teacher was away.
A sage who lived with his cart, sought out by a rich king.
A generous king who learned that generosity alone was not wisdom.
A poor scholar who, in a famine, questioned the priests at a king's sacrifice.
A teacher who showed his son the one reality with salt, seeds and water.
Uddalaka's son, who came home proud of his learning and was asked one question.
A learned sage who knew every subject and still had no peace.
The teacher who led Narada from names to the boundless.
The lord of creatures, who teaches Indra and Virochana about the self.
King of the gods, a student who kept doubting and kept coming back.
King of the asuras, who took the body to be the self and stopped asking.
A king who taught learned priests about the self of all.
The great sage of the Brihadaranyaka, husband of Maitreyi, debater at Janaka's court.
Yajnavalkya's wife, who turned down wealth and asked for what does not die.
A woman scholar who questioned Yajnavalkya twice before Janaka's assembly.
King of Videha, patron of learning and Yajnavalkya's student.
A proud scholar who offered to teach a king and ended up his student.
King of Kashi, who taught Balaki with a sleeping man.
The devas: Agni, Vayu, Indra and others, often shown as students.
The demons or anti-gods, cousins and rivals of the gods.
The radiant woman who tells Indra who the Yaksha was.
A mysterious being who appears before the gods and vanishes.
Varuna's son, who found the answer by thinking it through again and again.
Bhrigu's father and teacher, who answered every question with 'think more'.
A wealthy householder who asked what, once known, makes all things known.
The sage who made six seekers wait a year before answering them.
One of the six seekers before Pippalada.
One of the six seekers; he asks where creatures come from.
In the thunder story, the father of gods, humans and asuras.
The king whose sacrifice Ushasti attended.
A teacher named only through his mother, who took 'space' to mean the ordinary sky.
The unnamed teacher who gives a departing student his last instructions on how to live.
Speech, eye, ear, mind and breath, who quarrel over which of them is best.
Ushasti's young wife, who saved the leftover beans that fed him before the king's sacrifice.
Prachinashala, Satyayajna, Indradyumna, Jana and Budila: learned men who went to King Ashvapati to learn about the self of all.
Six learned seekers who came to Pippalada together, each with one question.
The one reality behind everything that is.
What you are, underneath body, mind and role.
Uddalaka's teaching that the subtle essence of all is your own self.
Saying what is so, and the real behind what seems.
Dying, what survives it, and Death as a teacher.
What does not die, and the wish to reach it.
Wanting, and what wanting does to us.
Two paths: what is good for you, and what feels good now.
How a teacher tests, waits and teaches.
Knowing about things, and knowing the imperishable.
Sacrifice and ceremony, and what they cannot give.
Looking again and again at what one takes oneself to be.
Food, the body it builds, and its place in the whole.
The breath that keeps us alive, chief among the powers.
Joy that does not depend on getting something.
The sacred syllable, a symbol of the whole.
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep and the fourth.
What dreams and deep sleep show about the self.
The light by which we see when sun and moon are gone.
The infinite, where nothing else is seen: the only true happiness.
Describing the self by saying what it is not.
The three lessons of the thunder.
Learning that begins when pride ends.
Body as chariot, senses as horses, mind as reins.
The one who watches without being touched.
Enjoying without grabbing; giving up what binds.
Everything is pervaded by the divine.
Truth, duty, care for parents, teachers and guests.
The universal self present in every person.
Holding something in mind as a way to the real.
vs: On the field of dharma, at Kurukshetra, my sons and the sons of Pandu gathered there eager to fight. What did they do, Sanjaya?
dhṛtarāṣṭra uvāca dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāścaiva kimakurvata saṃjaya 1-1
Seeing the Pandava army drawn up in battle order, King Duryodhana then went up to his teacher and spoke these words.
sañjaya uvāca dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṃ vyūḍhaṃ duryodhanastadā ācāryamupasaṃgamya rājā vacanamabravīt 1-2
Duryodhana said: Teacher, look at this vast army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, your own gifted pupil.
paśyaitāṃ pāṇḍuputrāṇāmācārya mahatīṃ camūm vyūḍhāṃ drupadaputreṇa tava śiṣyeṇa dhīmatā 1-3
Here are heroes, mighty archers equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna: Yuyudhana, Virata, and Drupada, a great chariot-warrior;
atra śūrā maheṣvāsā bhīmārjunasamā yudhi yuyudhāno virāṭaśca drupadaśca mahārathaḥ 1-4
Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana and the valiant king of Kashi; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, foremost among men;
dhṛṣṭaketuścekitānaḥ kāśirājaśca vīryavān purujitkuntibhojaśca śaibyaśca narapuṅgavaḥ 1-5
the bold Yudhamanyu and the valiant Uttamauja, the son of Subhadra, and the sons of Draupadi — every one of them a great chariot-warrior.
yudhāmanyuśca vikrānta uttamaujāśca vīryavān saubhadro draupadeyāśca sarva eva mahārathāḥ 1-6
Now hear, best of the twice-born, about the most distinguished on our side, the leaders of my army. I name them for you so you have them in mind.
asmākaṃ tu viśiṣṭā ye tānnibodha dvijottama nāyakā mama sainyasya saṃjñārthaṃ tānbravīmi te 1-7
Yourself, Bhishma, Karna, and Kripa, ever victorious in battle; Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and the son of Somadatta as well.
bhavānbhīṣmaśca karṇaśca kṛpaśca samitiṃjayaḥ aśvatthāmā vikarṇaśca saumadattistathaiva ca 1-8
And many other heroes, ready to give their lives for my sake, armed with many kinds of weapons and all skilled in war.
anye ca bahavaḥ śūrā madarthe tyaktajīvitāḥ nānāśastrapraharaṇāḥ sarve yuddhaviśāradāḥ 1-9
That strength of ours, guarded by Bhishma, is beyond measure, while their strength, guarded by Bhima, is limited.
aparyāptaṃ tadasmākaṃ balaṃ bhīṣmābhirakṣitam paryāptaṃ tvidameteṣāṃ balaṃ bhīmābhirakṣitam 1-10
So all of you, holding your assigned places at every point of entry, must above all protect Bhishma.
ayaneṣu ca sarveṣu yathābhāgamavasthitāḥ bhīṣmamevābhirakṣantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi 1-11
Then, to cheer him, the mighty grandsire, eldest of the Kurus, roared like a lion and blew his conch loudly.
tasya saṃjanayanharṣaṃ kuruvṛddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ siṃhanādaṃ vinadyoccaiḥ śaṅkhaṃ dadhmau pratāpavān 1-12
At once conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums and horns blared out together, and the sound was deafening.
tataḥ śaṅkhāśca bheryaśca paṇavānakagomukhāḥ sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śabdastumulo'bhavat 1-13
Then Madhava and the son of Pandu, standing in their great chariot yoked to white horses, blew their divine conches.
tataḥ śvetairhayairyukte mahati syandane sthitau mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaścaiva divyau śaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ 1-14
Hrishikesha blew Panchajanya, Dhananjaya blew Devadatta, and Vrikodara, doer of fearsome deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.
pāñcajanyaṃ hṛṣīkeśo devadattaṃ dhanañjayaḥ pauṇḍraṃ dadhmau mahāśaṅkhaṃ bhīmakarmā vṛkodaraḥ 1-15
King Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
anantavijayaṃ rājā kuntīputro yudhiṣṭhiraḥ nakulaḥ sahadevaśca sughoṣamaṇipuṣpakau 1-16
The king of Kashi, a superb archer, Shikhandi the great chariot-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquered Satyaki;
kāśyaśca parameṣvāsaḥ śikhaṇḍī ca mahārathaḥ dhṛṣṭadyumno virāṭaśca sātyakiścāparājitaḥ 1-17
Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the strong-armed son of Subhadra — all of them, lord of the earth, blew their own conches one after another.
drupado draupadeyāśca sarvaśaḥ pṛthivīpate saubhadraśca mahābāhuḥ śaṅkhāndadhmuḥ pṛthakpṛthak 1-18
That tumultuous roar, echoing through sky and earth, tore at the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons.
sa ghoṣo dhārtarāṣṭrāṇāṃ hṛdayāni vyadārayat nabhaśca pṛthivīṃ caiva tumulo vyanunādayan 1-19
Then, seeing Dhritarashtra's sons drawn up in position, as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the son of Pandu whose banner bears the monkey raised his bow…
atha vyavasthitāndṛṣṭvā dhārtarāṣṭrānkapidhvajaḥ pravṛtte śastrasaṃpāte dhanurudyamya pāṇḍavaḥ 1-20
…and, O king, spoke these words to Hrishikesha. Arjuna said: Achyuta, place my chariot between the two armies,
arjuna uvāca hṛṣīkeśaṃ tadā vākyamidamāha mahīpate senayorubhayormadhye rathaṃ sthāpaya me'cyuta 1-21
so that I may look over those who stand here eager for battle, and see whom I must fight in this coming war,
yāvadetānnirīkṣe'haṃ yoddhukāmānavasthitān kairmayā saha yoddhavyamasmin raṇasamudyame 1-22
and see those gathered here ready to fight, wishing in this war to please the wicked-minded son of Dhritarashtra.
yotsyamānānavekṣe'haṃ ya ete'tra samāgatāḥ dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddheryuddhe priyacikīrṣavaḥ 1-23
Addressed in this way by Gudakesha, O Bharata, Hrishikesha set the finest of chariots between the two armies,
sañjaya uvāca evamukto hṛṣīkeśo guḍākeśena bhārata senayorubhayormadhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam 1-24
facing Bhishma, Drona and all the rulers of the earth, and said: Partha, see these Kurus assembled here.
bhīṣmadroṇapramukhataḥ sarveṣāṃ ca mahīkṣitām uvāca pārtha paśyaitānsamavetānkurūniti 1-25
There Partha saw standing fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends,
tatrāpaśyatsthitānpārthaḥ pitṝnatha pitāmahān ācāryānmātulānbhrātṝnputrānpautrānsakhīṃstathā 1-26
fathers-in-law and well-wishers, in both the armies. Seeing all these kinsmen arrayed, the son of Kunti…
śvaśurānsuhṛdaścaiva senayorubhayorapi tānsamīkṣya sa kaunteyaḥ sarvānbandhūnavasthitān 1-27
…overcome with deep pity and sinking in sorrow, said this. Arjuna said: Krishna, seeing my own people standing here eager to fight,
arjuna uvāca kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdannidamabravīt dṛṣṭvemaṃ svajanaṃ kṛṣṇa yuyutsuṃ samupasthitam 1-28
my limbs give way and my mouth goes dry; my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṃ ca pariśuṣyati vepathuśca śarīre me romaharṣaśca jāyate 1-29
Gandiva is slipping from my hand, my skin is burning all over; I cannot stand steady, and my mind seems to be reeling.
gāṇḍīvaṃ sraṃsate hastāttvakcaiva paridahyate na ca śaknomyavasthātuṃ bhramatīva ca me manaḥ 1-30
I see ill omens, Keshava, and I see no good coming from killing my own people in battle.
nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni keśava na ca śreyo'nupaśyāmi hatvā svajanamāhave 1-31
I do not want victory, Krishna, nor a kingdom, nor pleasures. What use is a kingdom to us, Govinda, or enjoyments, or even life itself?
na kāṅkṣe vijayaṃ kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṃ sukhāni ca kiṃ no rājyena govinda kiṃ bhogairjīvitena vā 1-32
The very people for whose sake we wanted kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures stand here in battle, having staked their lives and wealth:
yeṣāmarthe kāṅkṣitaṃ no rājyaṃ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca ta ime'vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṃstyaktvā dhanāni ca 1-33
teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers too; maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other relatives.
ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrāstathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ saṃbandhinastathā 1-34
I do not wish to kill them, Madhusudana, even if they kill me — not even for rule over the three worlds, let alone for this earth.
etānna hantumicchāmi ghnato'pi madhusūdana api trailokyarājyasya hetoḥ kiṃ nu mahīkṛte 1-35
What joy could we have, Janardana, from killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Only sin would cling to us for slaying these aggressors.
nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrānnaḥ kā prītiḥ syājjanārdana pāpamevāśrayedasmānhatvaitānātatāyinaḥ 1-36
So it is not right for us to kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our own kinsmen. How could we be happy after killing our own people, Madhava?
tasmānnārhā vayaṃ hantuṃ dhārtarāṣṭrānsvabāndhavān svajanaṃ hi kathaṃ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava 1-37
Even if they, their minds overpowered by greed, do not see the evil in destroying a family or the sin in betraying friends,
yadyapyete na paśyanti lobhopahatacetasaḥ kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ mitradrohe ca pātakam 1-38
why should we, who clearly see the evil of destroying a family, not know enough to turn away from this sin, Janardana?
kathaṃ na jñeyamasmābhiḥ pāpādasmānnivartitum kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ prapaśyadbhirjanārdana 1-39
When a family is destroyed, its age-old family traditions perish; and when dharma is lost, lawlessness overwhelms the whole family.
kulakṣaye praṇaśyanti kuladharmāḥ sanātanāḥ dharme naṣṭe kulaṃ kṛtsnamadharmo'bhibhavatyuta 1-40
When lawlessness prevails, Krishna, the women of the family go astray; and when the women go astray, Varshneya, the social order is confused.
adharmābhibhavātkṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kulastriyaḥ strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇasaṃkaraḥ 1-41
This confusion leads both the family and its destroyers to hell, for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice and water.
saṃkaro narakāyaiva kulaghnānāṃ kulasya ca patanti pitaro hyeṣāṃ luptapiṇḍodakakriyāḥ 1-42
Through these wrongs of the family-destroyers, which cause confusion of the social order, the enduring duties of caste and family are swept away.
doṣairetaiḥ kulaghnānāṃ varṇasaṃkarakārakaiḥ utsādyante jātidharmāḥ kuladharmāśca śāśvatāḥ 1-43
We have heard, Janardana, that people whose family traditions have been destroyed dwell in hell for an indefinite time.
utsannakuladharmāṇāṃ manuṣyāṇāṃ janārdana narake'niyataṃ vāso bhavatītyanuśuśruma 1-44
Alas, what a great sin we have resolved to commit, setting out to kill our own people out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom!
aho bata mahatpāpaṃ kartuṃ vyavasitā vayam yadrājyasukhalobhena hantuṃ svajanamudyatāḥ 1-45
It would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle unarmed and unresisting.
yadi māmapratīkāramaśastraṃ śastrapāṇayaḥ dhārtarāṣṭrā raṇe hanyustanme kṣemataraṃ bhavet 1-46
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna cast aside his bow and arrows and sank down on the seat of the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
sañjaya uvāca evamuktvārjunaḥ saṃkhye rathopastha upāviśat visṛjya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ śokasaṃvignamānasaḥ 1-47
To him, overcome with pity, his eyes troubled and full of tears, sinking in despair, Madhusudana spoke these words.
sañjaya uvāca taṃ tathā kṛpayāviṣṭamaśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam viṣīdantamidaṃ vākyamuvāca madhusūdanaḥ 2-1
Where has this confusion come from, Arjuna, at such a critical moment? It is not fitting for a noble person; it leads neither to heaven nor to honour.
kutastvā kaśmalamidaṃ viṣame samupasthitam anāryajuṣṭamasvargyamakīrtikaramarjuna 2-2
Do not give in to unmanliness, Partha; it does not suit you. Cast off this petty faintness of heart and rise, scorcher of foes.
klaibyaṃ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitattvayyupapadyate kṣudraṃ hṛdayadaurbalyaṃ tyaktvottiṣṭha parantapa 2-3
Madhusudana, slayer of enemies, how can I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhishma and Drona, who deserve my reverence?
arjuna uvāca kathaṃ bhīṣmamahaṃ saṃkhye droṇaṃ ca madhusūdana iṣubhiḥ prati yotsyāmi pūjārhāvarisūdana 2-4
Better to live in this world even on begged food than to kill these noble elders. If I kill them, though they seek worldly gain, every pleasure I enjoy here will be stained with blood.
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān śreyo bhoktuṃ bhaikṣyamapīha loke hatvārthakāmāṃstu gurūnihaiva bhuñjīya bhogān rudhirapradigdhān 2-5
Nor do we know which is better for us — that we conquer them or that they conquer us. The sons of Dhritarashtra stand before us, and if we killed them we would not even wish to live.
na caitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣāma- ste'vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ 2-6

My nature is overcome by the flaw of faint-heartedness, and my mind is confused about dharma. I ask you: tell me clearly what is truly good for me. I am your disciple; I have come to you for refuge — guide me.
kārpaṇyadoṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ pṛcchāmi tvāṃ dharmasammūḍhacetāḥ yacchreyaḥ syānniścitaṃ brūhi tanme śiṣyaste'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam 2-7
I see nothing that could drive away this grief that is drying up my senses — not even gaining an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth, or lordship over the gods.
na hi prapaśyāmi mamāpanudyād yacchokamucchoṣaṇamindriyāṇām avāpya bhūmāvasapatnamṛddhaṃ rājyaṃ surāṇāmapi cādhipatyam 2-8
Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, O scorcher of foes, Gudakesha said to Govinda, “I will not fight,” and fell silent.
sañjaya uvāca evamuktvā hṛṣīkeśaṃ guḍākeśaḥ parantapa na yotsya iti govindamuktvā tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha 2-9
Then, O Bharata, between the two armies, Hrishikesha, as if smiling, spoke these words to the despairing Arjuna.
tamuvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasanniva bhārata senayorubhayormadhye viṣīdantamidaṃ vacaḥ 2-10
You grieve for those who need no grief, yet you speak words that sound wise. The truly wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
aśocyānanvaśocastvaṃ prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase gatāsūnagatāsūṃśca nānuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ 2-11
Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; nor will any of us ever cease to be hereafter.
na tvevāhaṃ jātu nāsaṃ na tvaṃ neme janādhipāḥ na caiva na bhaviṣyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param 2-12
Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not confused by this.
dehino'sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati 2-13
Contacts of the senses with their objects, son of Kunti, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last; bear them patiently, Bharata.
mātrāsparśāstu kaunteya śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkhadāḥ āgamāpāyino'nityāstāṃstitikṣasva bhārata 2-14
The steady person whom these do not disturb, finest of men, who stays the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality.
yaṃ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣaṃ puruṣarṣabha samaduḥkhasukhaṃ dhīraṃ so'mṛtatvāya kalpate 2-15
The unreal has no existence, and the real never ceases to be. Those who see the truth have understood the final nature of both.
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ ubhayorapi dṛṣṭo'ntastvanayostattvadarśibhiḥ 2-16
Know that what pervades all this is indestructible. No one can bring about the destruction of that which is imperishable.
avināśi tu tadviddhi yena sarvamidaṃ tatam vināśamavyayasyāsya na kaścitkartumarhati 2-17
These bodies are said to come to an end, but the embodied self within them is eternal, indestructible and beyond measure. Therefore fight, Bharata.
antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ anāśino'prameyasya tasmādyudhyasva bhārata 2-18
Whoever thinks this self is a killer, and whoever thinks it is killed — neither understands. It does not kill, and it is not killed.
ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaścainaṃ manyate hatam ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate 2-19

This self is not born and does not die. It did not begin at some point, and it will never come to an end. Without birth, lasting for ever, unchanging and older than time, it is not destroyed when the body is destroyed.
na jāyate mriyate vā kadācinnāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre 2-20
Partha, how can a person who knows this self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and unchanging cause anyone to be killed, or kill anyone?
vedāvināśinaṃ nityaṃ ya enamajamavyayam kathaṃ sa puruṣaḥ pārtha kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam 2-21
As a person discards worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self discards worn-out bodies and enters new ones.
vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naro'parāṇi tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇānyanyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī 2-22
Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it.
nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṃ dahati pāvakaḥ na cainaṃ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ 2-23
It cannot be cut, burned, wetted or dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, unmoving and timeless.
acchedyo'yamadāhyo'yamakledyo'śoṣya eva ca nityaḥ sarvagataḥ sthāṇuracalo'yaṃ sanātanaḥ 2-24
It is called unmanifest, beyond thought and unchanging. So, knowing it to be such, you should not grieve.
avyakto'yamacintyo'yamavikāryo'yamucyate tasmādevaṃ viditvainaṃ nānuśocitumarhasi 2-25
And even if you think it is constantly born and constantly dies, even then, mighty-armed one, you should not grieve like this.
atha cainaṃ nityajātaṃ nityaṃ vā manyase mṛtam tathāpi tvaṃ mahābāho naivaṃ śocitumarhasi 2-26
For death is certain for whoever is born, and birth is certain for whoever dies. So you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyurdhruvaṃ janma mṛtasya ca tasmādaparihārye'rthe na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi 2-27
Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle, and unmanifest again at their end, Bharata. What is there to lament in that?
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyaktamadhyāni bhārata avyaktanidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā 2-28
One person sees this self as a marvel, another speaks of it as a marvel, another hears of it as a marvel — and even after hearing of it, no one truly knows it.
āścaryavatpaśyati kaścidenamāścaryavadvadati tathaiva cānyaḥ āścaryavaccainamanyaḥ śṛṇoti śrutvāpyenaṃ veda na caiva kaścit 2-29
The self dwelling in every body can never be slain, Bharata. Therefore you should not grieve for any being.
dehī nityamavadhyo'yaṃ dehe sarvasya bhārata tasmātsarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi 2-30
Considering your own duty, too, you should not waver. For a kshatriya there is nothing better than a righteous war.
svadharmamapi cāvekṣya na vikampitumarhasi dharmyāddhi yuddhācchreyo'nyatkṣatriyasya na vidyate 2-31
Fortunate are the kshatriyas, Partha, who meet such a war, come of its own accord — an open door to heaven.
yadṛcchayā copapannaṃ svargadvāramapāvṛtam sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddhamīdṛśam 2-32
But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your duty and your honour, you will incur sin.
atha cettvamimaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃgrāmaṃ na kariṣyasi tataḥ svadharmaṃ kīrtiṃ ca hitvā pāpamavāpsyasi 2-33
People will tell of your disgrace forever, and for one who has been honoured, disgrace is worse than death.
akīrtiṃ cāpi bhūtāni kathayiṣyanti te'vyayām sambhāvitasya cākīrtirmaraṇādatiricyate 2-34
The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear, and those who held you in high regard will think little of you.
bhayādraṇāduparataṃ maṃsyante tvāṃ mahārathāḥ yeṣāṃ ca tvaṃ bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam 2-35
Your enemies will say many unspeakable things, mocking your strength. What could be more painful than that?
avācyavādāṃśca bahūnvadiṣyanti tavāhitāḥ nindantastava sāmarthyaṃ tato duḥkhataraṃ nu kim 2-36
Either you are killed and attain heaven, or you win and enjoy the earth. So rise, son of Kunti, resolved to fight.
hato vā prāpsyasi svargaṃ jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm tasmāduttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛtaniścayaḥ 2-37
Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, prepare for battle. In this way you will not incur sin.
sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṃ pāpamavāpsyasi 2-38
This understanding has been explained to you in terms of Sankhya; now hear it in terms of yoga. Joined with this understanding, Partha, you will throw off the bondage of action.
eṣā te'bhihitā sāṃkhye buddhiryoge tvimāṃ śṛṇu buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha karmabandhaṃ prahāsyasi 2-39
On this path no effort is lost and no reverse occurs. Even a little of this practice protects one from great fear.
nehābhikramanāśo'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate svalpamapyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt 2-40
Here, joy of the Kurus, the resolute understanding is single; but the thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
vyavasāyātmikā buddhirekeha kurunandana bahuśākhā hyanantāśca buddhayo'vyavasāyinām 2-41
Partha, the unwise utter flowery words; delighting in the letter of the Vedas, they declare there is nothing else.
yāmimāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadantyavipaścitaḥ vedavādaratāḥ pārtha nānyadastīti vādinaḥ 2-42
Full of desire and intent on heaven, they speak of many special rites that promise rebirth as the fruit of action and aim at enjoyment and power.
kāmātmānaḥ svargaparā janmakarmaphalapradām kriyāviśeṣabahulāṃ bhogaiśvaryagatiṃ prati 2-43
Those attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by such talk, do not develop the resolute understanding that rests in meditation.
bhogaiśvaryaprasaktānāṃ tayāpahṛtacetasām vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate 2-44
The Vedas deal with the three gunas; Arjuna, rise above the three gunas. Be free of the pairs of opposites, always rooted in purity, unconcerned with getting and keeping, and centred in the self.
traiguṇyaviṣayā vedā nistraiguṇyo bhavārjuna nirdvandvo nityasattvastho niryogakṣema ātmavān 2-45
As much use as a small well has when water floods everywhere, so much use have all the Vedas for a brahmin who truly knows.
yāvānartha udapāne sarvataḥ saṃplutodake tāvānsarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ 2-46
Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to inaction.
karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo'stvakarmaṇi 2-47
Established in yoga, do your work, Dhananjaya, giving up attachment and staying even-minded in success and failure. This evenness is called yoga.
yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanaṃjaya siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate 2-48
Mere action is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, Dhananjaya. Seek refuge in that understanding; pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit.
dūreṇa hyavaraṃ karma buddhiyogāddhanaṃjaya buddhau śaraṇamanviccha kṛpaṇāḥ phalahetavaḥ 2-49
One joined with this understanding leaves behind both good and bad deeds here. So devote yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
buddhiyukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛtaduṣkṛte tasmādyogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam 2-50
The wise, joined with this understanding, give up the fruit born of action, and, freed from the bondage of birth, reach the state beyond all suffering.
karmajaṃ buddhiyuktā hi phalaṃ tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ janmabandhavinirmuktāḥ padaṃ gacchantyanāmayam 2-51
When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, you will become indifferent to what you have heard and what is yet to be heard.
yadā te mohakalilaṃ buddhirvyatitariṣyati tadā gantāsi nirvedaṃ śrotavyasya śrutasya ca 2-52
When your understanding, now unsettled by conflicting teachings, stands firm and unmoving in meditative absorption, then you will attain yoga.
śrutivipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niścalā samādhāvacalā buddhistadā yogamavāpsyasi 2-53
Keshava, how is one of steady wisdom, settled in meditation, described? How does a person of steady mind speak, how does he sit, how does he move?
arjuna uvāca sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava sthitadhīḥ kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajeta kim 2-54
Partha, when a person gives up every desire that arises in the mind and is content in the self, by the self alone, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
prajahāti yadā kāmānsarvānpārtha manogatān ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate 2-55
One whose mind is not shaken in sorrow, who does not crave pleasures, who is free from passion, fear and anger — such a sage is called steady of mind.
duḥkheṣvanudvignamanāḥ sukheṣu vigataspṛhaḥ vītarāgabhayakrodhaḥ sthitadhīrmunirucyate 2-56
One who is unattached everywhere, who neither rejoices on meeting good nor resents meeting bad — his wisdom is firmly established.
yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehastattatprāpya śubhāśubham nābhinandati na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā 2-57
When he draws his senses back from their objects on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly established.
yadā saṃharate cāyaṃ kūrmo'ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā 2-58
Sense objects fall away from one who abstains from them, but the taste for them remains; even that taste fades once the Supreme is seen.
viṣayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ rasavarjaṃ raso'pyasya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate 2-59
For the turbulent senses, son of Kunti, forcibly carry off the mind even of a wise person who is striving.
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ 2-60
Restraining them all, one should sit disciplined, intent on me. One whose senses are under control has firm wisdom.
tāni sarvāṇi saṃyamya yukta āsīta matparaḥ vaśe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā 2-61
When a person dwells on sense objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger.
dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate saṅgātsaṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho'bhijāyate 2-62
Anger breeds delusion, and delusion confuses memory; when memory fails, understanding is ruined, and when understanding is ruined, a person is lost.
krodhādbhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ smṛtibhraṃśādbuddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati 2-63
But the self-controlled person, moving among sense objects with senses free from attraction and aversion and under the control of the self, attains inner calm.
rāgadveṣaviyuktaistu viṣayānindriyaiścaran ātmavaśyairvidheyātmā prasādamadhigacchati 2-64
In that calm all his sorrows come to an end, for the understanding of one whose mind is serene soon becomes firmly settled.
prasāde sarvaduḥkhānāṃ hānirasyopajāyate prasannacetaso hyāśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate 2-65
The undisciplined have no settled understanding, and no power of contemplation; without contemplation there is no peace, and without peace how can there be happiness?
nāsti buddhirayuktasya na cāyuktasya bhāvanā na cābhāvayataḥ śāntiraśāntasya kutaḥ sukham 2-66
When the mind follows the roaming senses, it carries away one's wisdom, as wind carries off a boat on the water.
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nu vidhīyate tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi 2-67
Therefore, mighty-armed one, one whose senses are fully held back from their objects has firmly established wisdom.
tasmādyasya mahābāho nigṛhītāni sarvaśaḥ indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā 2-68
What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake to; and that in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ 2-69
As waters flow into the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays steady within its bounds, so one into whom all desires enter in the same way attains peace — not one who chases desires.
āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī 2-70
The person who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing, without any sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.
vihāya kāmānyaḥ sarvān pumāṃścarati niḥspṛhaḥ nirmamo nirahaṃkāraḥ sa śāntimadhigacchati 2-71
This is the state of Brahman, Partha; having reached it, one is no longer deluded. Remaining in it even at the hour of death, one attains the peace of Brahman.
eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati sthitvāsyāmantakāle'pi brahmanirvāṇamṛcchati 2-72
Janardana, if you hold that understanding is higher than action, then why, Keshava, do you push me into this terrible deed?
arjuna uvāca jyāyasī cetkarmaṇaste matā buddhirjanārdana tatkiṃ karmaṇi ghore māṃ niyojayasi keśava 3-1
Your words seem to pull in two directions, and they leave my understanding confused. Tell me plainly the one path, settled for certain, by which I may reach the highest good.
vyāmiśreṇeva vākyena buddhiṃ mohayasīva me tadekaṃ vada niścitya yena śreyo'hamāpnuyām 3-2
Sinless one, long ago I taught that in this world there are two ways of steady practice: the path of knowledge for those given to reflection, and the path of action for those given to yoga.
loke'smindvividhā niṣṭhā purā proktā mayānagha jñānayogena sāṃkhyānāṃ karmayogena yoginām 3-3
A person does not reach freedom from action merely by not starting any work, nor does one attain perfection by renunciation alone.
na karmaṇāmanārambhānnaiṣkarmyaṃ puruṣo'śnute na ca saṃnyasanādeva siddhiṃ samadhigacchati 3-4
No one can stay without acting even for a moment; every being is driven to act, whether it wants to or not, by the qualities (gunas) born of nature (Prakriti).
na hi kaścitkṣaṇamapi jātu tiṣṭhatyakarmakṛt kāryate hyavaśaḥ karma sarvaḥ prakṛtijairguṇaiḥ 3-5
One who holds back the organs of action but sits dwelling in the mind on the objects of the senses is deluded, and is called a pretender.
karmendriyāṇi saṃyamya ya āste manasā smaran indriyārthānvimūḍhātmā mithyācāraḥ sa ucyate 3-6
But one who reins in the senses with the mind, Arjuna, and without attachment takes up the yoga of action through the organs of action, stands far above.
yastvindriyāṇi manasā niyamyārabhate'rjuna karmendriyaiḥ karmayogamasaktaḥ sa viśiṣyate 3-7
Do the work that is yours to do, for action is better than inaction; without acting you could not even keep your body going.
niyataṃ kuru karma tvaṃ karma jyāyo hyakarmaṇaḥ śarīrayātrāpi ca te na prasiddhyedakarmaṇaḥ 3-8
This world is bound by action, except action done as sacrifice. So, son of Kunti, act for that purpose, free of attachment.
yajñārthātkarmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karmabandhanaḥ tadarthaṃ karma kaunteya muktasaṅgaḥ samācara 3-9
In the beginning, the Lord of creatures brought forth beings together with sacrifice and said: "Through this you will multiply; let this be the cow that yields all you wish for."
sahayajñāḥ prajāḥ sṛṣṭvā purovāca prajāpatiḥ anena prasaviṣyadhvameṣa vo'stviṣṭakāmadhuk 3-10
"Nourish the gods with this, and let the gods nourish you. Sustaining one another, you will reach the highest good."
devānbhāvayatānena te devā bhāvayantu vaḥ parasparaṃ bhāvayantaḥ śreyaḥ paramavāpsyatha 3-11
"Pleased by sacrifice, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire." One who enjoys their gifts without offering anything back to them is nothing but a thief.
iṣṭānbhogānhi vo devā dāsyante yajñabhāvitāḥ tairdattānapradāyaibhyo yo bhuṅkte stena eva saḥ 3-12
The good, who eat what remains after sacrifice, are released from all faults; but the wicked who cook only for themselves eat their own sin.
yajñaśiṣṭāśinaḥ santo mucyante sarvakilbiṣaiḥ bhuñjate te tvaghaṃ pāpā ye pacantyātmakāraṇāt 3-13
Beings arise from food, food comes from rain, rain comes from sacrifice, and sacrifice is born of action.
annādbhavanti bhūtāni parjanyādannasambhavaḥ yajñādbhavati parjanyo yajñaḥ karmasamudbhavaḥ 3-14
Know that action springs from the Veda, and the Veda springs from the Imperishable. So the all-pervading Brahman is always present in sacrifice.
karma brahmodbhavaṃ viddhi brahmākṣarasamudbhavam tasmātsarvagataṃ brahma nityaṃ yajñe pratiṣṭhitam 3-15
Partha, whoever in this world does not keep turning the wheel set in motion this way, living in sin and taking delight only in the senses, lives in vain.
evaṃ pravartitaṃ cakraṃ nānuvartayatīha yaḥ aghāyurindriyārāmo moghaṃ pārtha sa jīvati 3-16
But for the person whose joy is in the Self alone, who is fulfilled in the Self and content in the Self, there remains no duty to perform.
yastvātmaratireva syādātmatṛptaśca mānavaḥ ātmanyeva ca santuṣṭastasya kāryaṃ na vidyate 3-17
Such a one gains nothing here by acting and loses nothing by not acting, and depends on no being for any purpose.
naiva tasya kṛtenārtho nākṛteneha kaścana na cāsya sarvabhūteṣu kaścidarthavyapāśrayaḥ 3-18
So always do the work that must be done, without attachment; by acting unattached a person reaches the Supreme.
tasmādasaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara asakto hyācarankarma paramāpnoti pūruṣaḥ 3-19
Janaka and others reached perfection through action alone. And looking to the welfare of the world too, you should act.
karmaṇaiva hi saṃsiddhimāsthitā janakādayaḥ lokasaṃgrahamevāpi saṃpaśyankartumarhasi 3-20
Whatever a leading person does, others do the same; whatever standard such a person sets, the world follows.
yadyadācarati śreṣṭhastattadevetaro janaḥ sa yatpramāṇaṃ kurute lokastadanuvartate 3-21
Partha, there is nothing in the three worlds that I must do, nothing I lack that I need to gain; and yet I go on acting.
na me pārthāsti kartavyaṃ triṣu lokeṣu kiṃcana nānavāptamavāptavyaṃ varta eva ca karmaṇi 3-22
For if I ever stopped acting tirelessly, Partha, people everywhere would follow my path.
yadi hyahaṃ na varteyaṃ jātu karmaṇyatandritaḥ mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ 3-23
If I did not work, these worlds would fall into ruin; I would be the cause of confusion and would bring these beings to destruction.
utsīdeyurime lokā na kuryāṃ karma cedaham saṃkarasya ca kartā syāmupahanyāmimāḥ prajāḥ 3-24
Bharata, just as the unwise act out of attachment to their work, the wise should act without attachment, wishing to hold the world together.
saktāḥ karmaṇyavidvāṃso yathā kurvanti bhārata kuryādvidvāṃstathāsaktaścikīrṣurlokasaṃgraham 3-25
The wise should not unsettle the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action. Acting with discipline themselves, they should lead others to take joy in all their work.
na buddhibhedaṃ janayedajñānāṃ karmasaṅginām joṣayetsarvakarmāṇi vidvānyuktaḥ samācaran 3-26
All actions are carried out entirely by the qualities of nature, but one whose mind is clouded by ego thinks, "I am the doer."
prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ ahaṃkāravimūḍhātmā kartāhamiti manyate 3-27
But one who knows the truth about how the qualities and their actions are divided, mighty-armed one, understands that it is qualities acting upon qualities, and does not become attached.
tattvavittu mahābāho guṇakarmavibhāgayoḥ guṇā guṇeṣu vartanta iti matvā na sajjate 3-28
Those deluded by the qualities of nature cling to the workings of those qualities. One who knows the whole should not unsettle such slow people who know only in part.
prakṛterguṇasaṃmūḍhāḥ sajjante guṇakarmasu tānakṛtsnavido mandānkṛtsnavinna vicālayet 3-29
Hand over all your actions to me, with your mind fixed on the Self; free of craving and of the sense of "mine", and with your fever gone, fight.
mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasyādhyātmacetasā nirāśīrnirmamo bhūtvā yudhyasva vigatajvaraḥ 3-30
Those who always follow this teaching of mine with faith and without finding fault are also released from the bonds of action.
ye me matamidaṃ nityamanutiṣṭhanti mānavāḥ śraddhāvanto'nasūyanto mucyante te'pi karmabhiḥ 3-31
But those who scoff at it and do not follow my teaching, know them to be confused about all knowledge, senseless and lost.
ye tvetadabhyasūyanto nānutiṣṭhanti me matam sarvajñānavimūḍhāṃstānviddhi naṣṭānacetasaḥ 3-32
Even a knowing person acts in keeping with their own nature. All beings follow their nature; what can forcing it achieve?
sadṛśaṃ ceṣṭate svasyāḥ prakṛterjñānavānapi prakṛtiṃ yānti bhūtāni nigrahaḥ kiṃ kariṣyati 3-33
Liking and disliking are firmly seated in each sense with regard to its objects. Do not fall under their sway, for they are enemies on one's path.
indriyasyendriyasyārthe rāgadveṣau vyavasthitau tayorna vaśamāgacchettau hyasya paripanthinau 3-34
Better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's dharma done well. Better to die in one's own dharma; another's dharma brings danger.
śreyānsvadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmātsvanuṣṭhitāt svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ paradharmo bhayāvahaḥ 3-35
Then what drives a person to do wrong, Varshneya, even against their own wish, as if pushed into it by force?
arjuna uvāca atha kena prayukto'yaṃ pāpaṃ carati pūruṣaḥ anicchannapi vārṣṇeya balādiva niyojitaḥ 3-36
It is desire, it is anger, born of the quality of passion; it devours without end and is the great evil. Know it as the enemy here.
kāma eṣa krodha eṣa rajoguṇasamudbhavaḥ mahāśano mahāpāpmā viddhyenamiha vairiṇam 3-37
As fire is hidden by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo by its membrane, so is this covered by desire.
dhūmenāvriyate vahniryathādarśo malena ca yatholbenāvṛto garbhastathā tenedamāvṛtam 3-38
Son of Kunti, knowledge is veiled by this constant enemy of the wise, which takes the form of desire, never satisfied, like fire.
āvṛtaṃ jñānametena jñānino nityavairiṇā kāmarūpeṇa kaunteya duṣpūreṇānalena ca 3-39
The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its dwelling. Through them it veils knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
indriyāṇi mano buddhirasyādhiṣṭhānamucyate etairvimohayatyeṣa jñānamāvṛtya dehinam 3-40
So, best of the Bharatas, first bring the senses under control, and then destroy this evil thing that ruins both knowledge and realisation.
tasmāttvamindriyāṇyādau niyamya bharatarṣabha pāpmānaṃ prajahi hyenaṃ jñānavijñānanāśanam 3-41
The senses are called higher than the body; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; and higher than the intellect is the Self.
indriyāṇi parāṇyāhurindriyebhyaḥ paraṃ manaḥ manasastu parā buddhiryo buddheḥ paratastu saḥ 3-42
Knowing in this way what lies beyond the intellect, steady yourself by the Self, mighty-armed one, and kill this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome.
evaṃ buddheḥ paraṃ buddhvā saṃstabhyātmānamātmanā jahi śatruṃ mahābāho kāmarūpaṃ durāsadam 3-43
I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvan; Vivasvan passed it to Manu, and Manu told it to Ikshvaku.
imaṃ vivasvate yogaṃ proktavānahamavyayam vivasvānmanave prāha manurikṣvākave'bravīt 4-1
Handed down in this way from one to the next, it was known to the royal sages. But over a long stretch of time, scorcher of foes, this yoga was lost here.
evaṃ paramparāprāptamimaṃ rājarṣayo viduḥ sa kāleneha mahatā yogo naṣṭaḥ parantapa 4-2
That same ancient yoga I have told you today, because you are my devotee and my friend; this is indeed the highest secret.
sa evāyaṃ mayā te'dya yogaḥ proktaḥ purātanaḥ bhakto'si me sakhā ceti rahasyaṃ hyetaduttamam 4-3
Your birth is recent, and Vivasvan's birth was long ago. How am I to understand that you taught it at the beginning?
arjuna uvāca aparaṃ bhavato janma paraṃ janma vivasvataḥ kathametadvijānīyāṃ tvamādau proktavāniti 4-4
Many births of mine have passed, Arjuna, and many of yours too. I know them all, but you do not, scorcher of foes.
bahūni me vyatītāni janmāni tava cārjuna tānyahaṃ veda sarvāṇi na tvaṃ vettha parantapa 4-5
Though I am unborn and my being never perishes, and though I am the Lord of all beings, I take birth by governing my own nature through my own power of maya.
ajo'pi sannavyayātmā bhūtānāmīśvaro'pi san prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya saṃbhavāmyātmamāyayā 4-6
Whenever righteousness declines, Bharata, and unrighteousness rises, then I bring myself forth.
yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānirbhavati bhārata abhyutthānamadharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmyaham 4-7
To protect the good, to destroy those who do evil, and to establish righteousness firmly again, I come into being age after age.
paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām dharmasaṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge 4-8
One who truly understands my divine birth and action in this way is not born again on leaving the body, but comes to me, Arjuna.
janma karma ca me divyamevaṃ yo vetti tattvataḥ tyaktvā dehaṃ punarjanma naiti māmeti so'rjuna 4-9
Free from craving, fear and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, many, purified by the discipline of knowledge, have reached my state of being.
vītarāgabhayakrodhā manmayā māmupāśritāḥ bahavo jñānatapasā pūtā madbhāvamāgatāḥ 4-10
In whatever way people come to me, in that very way I receive them. Everywhere, Partha, people follow my path.
ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃstathaiva bhajāmyaham mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ 4-11
Wanting success in their work, people here worship the gods, for in the human world success that comes from action arrives quickly.
kāṅkṣantaḥ karmaṇāṃ siddhiṃ yajanta iha devatāḥ kṣipraṃ hi mānuṣe loke siddhirbhavati karmajā 4-12
The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions. Though I am its maker, know me as the unchanging non-doer.
cāturvarṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇakarmavibhāgaśaḥ tasya kartāramapi māṃ viddhyakartāramavyayam 4-13
Actions do not stain me, nor do I long for their fruit. One who knows me in this way is not bound by actions.
na māṃ karmāṇi limpanti na me karmaphale spṛhā iti māṃ yo'bhijānāti karmabhirna sa badhyate 4-14
Knowing this, the seekers of freedom of old also acted. So you too should act, as the ancients did long before.
evaṃ jñātvā kṛtaṃ karma pūrvairapi mumukṣubhiḥ kuru karmaiva tasmāttvaṃ pūrvaiḥ pūrvataraṃ kṛtam 4-15
What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused about this. So I will explain action to you, and knowing it you will be freed from what is harmful.
kiṃ karma kimakarmeti kavayo'pyatra mohitāḥ tatte karma pravakṣyāmi yajjñātvā mokṣyase'śubhāt 4-16
One must understand what action is, understand what wrong action is, and understand what inaction is; the way of action is deep.
karmaṇo hyapi boddhavyaṃ boddhavyaṃ ca vikarmaṇaḥ akarmaṇaśca boddhavyaṃ gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ 4-17
One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among people; that person is steady in yoga and does every action fully.
karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyedakarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ sa buddhimānmanuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsnakarmakṛt 4-18
One whose every undertaking is free of desire and selfish intention, whose actions are burned up in the fire of knowledge, is called learned by the wise.
yasya sarve samārambhāḥ kāmasaṃkalpavarjitāḥ jñānāgnidagdhakarmāṇaṃ tamāhuḥ paṇḍitaṃ budhāḥ 4-19
Letting go of attachment to the fruit of action, always content and depending on nothing, such a person does nothing at all even while fully engaged in action.
tyaktvā karmaphalāsaṅgaṃ nityatṛpto nirāśrayaḥ karmaṇyabhipravṛtto'pi naiva kiṃcitkaroti saḥ 4-20
Without craving, with mind and body held in check, giving up all possessiveness, doing only the work the body needs, one incurs no sin.
nirāśīryatacittātmā tyaktasarvaparigrahaḥ śārīraṃ kevalaṃ karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam 4-21
Content with whatever comes by chance, beyond the pairs of opposites, free of envy, and even-minded in success and failure, one is not bound even when acting.
yadṛcchālābhasaṃtuṣṭo dvandvātīto vimatsaraḥ samaḥ siddhāvasiddhau ca kṛtvāpi na nibadhyate 4-22
For one who is unattached and free, whose mind is settled in knowledge, and who acts for the sake of sacrifice, all action melts away completely.
gatasaṅgasya muktasya jñānāvasthitacetasaḥ yajñāyācarataḥ karma samagraṃ pravilīyate 4-23
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. One who sees Brahman in all action reaches Brahman alone.
brahmārpaṇaṃ brahma havirbrahmāgnau brahmaṇā hutam brahmaiva tena gantavyaṃ brahmakarmasamādhinā 4-24
Some yogis perform sacrifice to the gods alone; others offer sacrifice itself as an oblation into the fire of Brahman.
daivamevāpare yajñaṃ yoginaḥ paryupāsate brahmāgnāvapare yajñaṃ yajñenaivopajuhvati 4-25
Some offer hearing and the other senses into the fires of restraint; others offer sound and the other objects into the fires of the senses.
śrotrādīnīndriyāṇyanye saṃyamāgniṣu juhvati śabdādīnviṣayānanya indriyāgniṣu juhvati 4-26
Others offer all the workings of the senses and of the life-breath into the fire of the yoga of self-control, kindled by knowledge.
sarvāṇīndriyakarmāṇi prāṇakarmāṇi cāpare ātmasaṃyamayogāgnau juhvati jñānadīpite 4-27
Some offer wealth as sacrifice, some austerity, some the practice of yoga; and other striving people of firm vows offer study of scripture and knowledge.
dravyayajñāstapoyajñā yogayajñāstathāpare svādhyāyajñānayajñāśca yatayaḥ saṃśitavratāḥ 4-28
Others, devoted to breath control, offer the in-breath into the out-breath and the out-breath into the in-breath, restraining the flow of both.
apāne juhvati prāṇaṃ prāṇe'pānaṃ tathāpare prāṇāpānagatī ruddhvā prāṇāyāmaparāyaṇāḥ 4-29
Others, eating in measure, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths. All of these know what sacrifice is, and through sacrifice their impurities are worn away.
apare niyatāhārāḥ prāṇānprāṇeṣu juhvati sarve'pyete yajñavido yajñakṣapitakalmaṣāḥ 4-30
Those who eat the nectar left over from sacrifice reach the eternal Brahman. This world is not for one who makes no sacrifice, best of the Kurus; how then the other?
yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujo yānti brahma sanātanam nāyaṃ loko'styayajñasya kuto'nyaḥ kurusattama 4-31
In this way many kinds of sacrifice are laid out in the words of the Veda. Know that all of them are born of action; knowing this, you will be set free.
evaṃ bahuvidhā yajñā vitatā brahmaṇo mukhe karmajānviddhi tānsarvānevaṃ jñātvā vimokṣyase 4-32
Scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is better than any sacrifice of material things; for all action, Partha, finds its completion in knowledge.
śreyāndravyamayādyajñājjñānayajñaḥ parantapa sarvaṃ karmākhilaṃ pārtha jñāne parisamāpyate 4-33
Learn it by bowing down, by sincere questioning, and by service. The wise who have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.
tadviddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā upadekṣyanti te jñānaṃ jñāninastattvadarśinaḥ 4-34
Knowing that, Pandava, you will not fall into such confusion again, and through it you will see all beings without exception in yourself, and then in me.
yajjñātvā na punarmohamevaṃ yāsyasi pāṇḍava yena bhūtānyaśeṣeṇa drakṣyasyātmanyatho mayi 4-35
Even if you were the worst of all sinners, you would cross over every wrong by the boat of knowledge alone.
api cedasi pāpebhyaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpakṛttamaḥ sarvaṃ jñānaplavenaiva vṛjinaṃ santariṣyasi 4-36
Arjuna, as a blazing fire turns firewood to ash, so the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash.
yathaidhāṃsi samiddho'gnirbhasmasātkurute'rjuna jñānāgniḥ sarvakarmāṇi bhasmasātkurute tathā 4-37
Truly, nothing in this world purifies like knowledge. One who is perfected in yoga finds it in oneself, in time.
na hi jñānena sadṛśaṃ pavitramiha vidyate tatsvayaṃ yogasaṃsiddhaḥ kālenātmani vindati 4-38
One who has faith, who is devoted to it and has mastered the senses, gains knowledge; and having gained it, soon reaches supreme peace.
śraddhāvā~llabhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntimacireṇādhigacchati 4-39
But one who is ignorant, without faith and full of doubt is ruined. For the doubter there is neither this world nor the next, nor any happiness.
ajñaścāśraddadhānaśca saṃśayātmā vinaśyati nāyaṃ loko'sti na paro na sukhaṃ saṃśayātmanaḥ 4-40
Actions do not bind one who has given up action through yoga, whose doubts are cut away by knowledge, and who is established in the Self, Dhananjaya.
yogasaṃnyastakarmāṇaṃ jñānasaṃchinnasaṃśayam ātmavantaṃ na karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanaṃjaya 4-41
So, Bharata, cut through this doubt in your heart, born of ignorance, with the sword of knowledge of the Self. Take refuge in yoga, and stand up.
tasmādajñānasambhūtaṃ hṛtsthaṃ jñānāsinātmanaḥ chittvainaṃ saṃśayaṃ yogamātiṣṭhottiṣṭha bhārata 4-42
Krishna, you praise the renunciation of action, and then again the yoga of action. Tell me with certainty which one of the two is better.
arjuna uvāca saṃnyāsaṃ karmaṇāṃ kṛṣṇa punaryogaṃ ca śaṃsasi yacchreya etayorekaṃ tanme brūhi suniścitam 5-1
Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good, but of the two, the yoga of action is better than renouncing action.
saṃnyāsaḥ karmayogaśca niḥśreyasakarāvubhau tayostu karmasaṃnyāsātkarmayogo viśiṣyate 5-2
Know that person as a true renunciant at all times who neither hates nor craves; free of the pairs of opposites, mighty-armed one, they are easily released from bondage.
jñeyaḥ sa nityasaṃnyāsī yo na dveṣṭi na kāṅkṣati nirdvandvo hi mahābāho sukhaṃ bandhātpramucyate 5-3
Only the naive, not the wise, speak of the path of knowledge and the path of yoga as different. One who is truly settled in either one gains the fruit of both.
sāṃkhyayogau pṛthagbālāḥ pravadanti na paṇḍitāḥ ekamapyāsthitaḥ samyagubhayorvindate phalam 5-4
The state reached by the followers of knowledge is reached by the followers of yoga as well. One who sees knowledge and yoga as one truly sees.
yatsāṃkhyaiḥ prāpyate sthānaṃ tadyogairapi gamyate ekaṃ sāṃkhyaṃ ca yogaṃ ca yaḥ paśyati saḥ paśyati 5-5
But renunciation, mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga; a sage who is steady in yoga reaches Brahman before long.
saṃnyāsastu mahābāho duḥkhamāptumayogataḥ yogayukto munirbrahma nacireṇādhigacchati 5-6
Steady in yoga, pure in heart, master of mind and senses, whose self has become the self of all beings, such a person is not stained even while acting.
yogayukto viśuddhātmā vijitātmā jitendriyaḥ sarvabhūtātmabhūtātmā kurvannapi na lipyate 5-7
One who is steady and knows the truth thinks, "I do nothing at all," even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping and breathing…
naiva kiṃcitkaromīti yukto manyeta tattvavit paśyañśṛṇvanspṛśañjighrannaśnangacchansvapañśvasan 5-8
…while speaking, letting go, taking hold, opening and closing the eyes, holding firmly that it is only the senses moving among their objects.
pralapanvisṛjangṛhṇannunmiṣannimiṣannapi indriyāṇīndriyārtheṣu vartanta iti dhārayan 5-9
One who acts by placing all actions in Brahman and giving up attachment is not touched by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
brahmaṇyādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ lipyate na sa pāpena padmapatramivāmbhasā 5-10
Giving up attachment, yogis act with the body, the mind, the intellect, and even the senses alone, for the purification of the self.
kāyena manasā buddhyā kevalairindriyairapi yoginaḥ karma kurvanti saṅgaṃ tyaktvātmaśuddhaye 5-11
One who is steady gives up the fruit of action and attains lasting peace; one who is not, driven by desire and attached to the fruit, is bound.
yuktaḥ karmaphalaṃ tyaktvā śāntimāpnoti naiṣṭhikīm ayuktaḥ kāmakāreṇa phale sakto nibadhyate 5-12
Having given up all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing anything to be done.
sarvakarmāṇi manasā saṃnyasyāste sukhaṃ vaśī navadvāre pure dehī naiva kurvanna kārayan 5-13
The Lord does not create agency for the world, nor actions, nor the link between action and its fruit; it is nature that carries all this on.
na kartṛtvaṃ na karmāṇi lokasya sṛjati prabhuḥ na karmaphalasaṃyogaṃ svabhāvastu pravartate 5-14
The all-pervading one takes on no one's sin and no one's good deed either. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and that is why beings are deluded.
nādatte kasyacitpāpaṃ na caiva sukṛtaṃ vibhuḥ ajñānenāvṛtaṃ jñānaṃ tena muhyanti jantavaḥ 5-15
But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge shines like the sun and reveals the Supreme.
jñānena tu tadajñānaṃ yeṣāṃ nāśitamātmanaḥ teṣāmādityavajjñānaṃ prakāśayati tatparam 5-16
With their intellect on That, their self in That, their devotion in That and That as their final goal, their impurities shaken off by knowledge, they go to the state from which there is no return.
tadbuddhayastadātmānastanniṣṭhāstatparāyaṇāḥ gacchantyapunarāvṛttiṃ jñānanirdhūtakalmaṣāḥ 5-17
The wise look with an equal eye on a learned and humble Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste who eats dogs.
vidyāvinayasaṃpanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini śuni caiva śvapāke ca paṇḍitāḥ samadarśinaḥ 5-18
Those whose mind rests in equality have conquered the cycle of birth here and now. Brahman is flawless and the same in all, so they are established in Brahman.
ihaiva tairjitaḥ sargo yeṣāṃ sāmye sthitaṃ manaḥ nirdoṣaṃ hi samaṃ brahma tasmādbrahmaṇi te sthitāḥ 5-19
With steady understanding and free of delusion, the knower of Brahman, established in Brahman, does not rejoice on getting what is pleasant or recoil on meeting what is unpleasant.
na prahṛṣyetpriyaṃ prāpya nodvijetprāpya cāpriyam sthirabuddhirasaṃmūḍho brahmavidbrahmaṇi sthitaḥ 5-20
One whose self is unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that lies within. United with Brahman through yoga, that person enjoys a happiness that never fades.
bāhyasparśeṣvasaktātmā vindatyātmani yat sukham sa brahmayogayuktātmā sukhamakṣayamaśnute 5-21
The pleasures born of contact with objects are only sources of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, son of Kunti, and the wise take no delight in them.
ye hi saṃsparśajā bhogā duḥkhayonaya eva te ādyantavantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ 5-22
One who can withstand, right here before leaving the body, the surge that comes from desire and anger is steady in yoga; that person is happy.
śaknotīhaiva yaḥ soḍhuṃ prākśarīravimokṣaṇāt kāmakrodhodbhavaṃ vegaṃ sa yuktaḥ sa sukhī naraḥ 5-23
One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and attains the peace of Brahman.
yo'ntaḥsukho'ntarārāmastathāntarjyotireva yaḥ sa yogī brahmanirvāṇaṃ brahmabhūto'dhigacchati 5-24
Seers whose faults are worn away, whose doubts are cut, who are self-controlled and devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain the peace of Brahman.
labhante brahmanirvāṇamṛṣayaḥ kṣīṇakalmaṣāḥ chinnadvaidhā yatātmānaḥ sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ 5-25
For the self-disciplined who are free of desire and anger, who have mastered their thoughts and know the Self, the peace of Brahman is near on every side.
kāmakrodhaviyuktānāṃ yatīnāṃ yatacetasām abhito brahmanirvāṇaṃ vartate viditātmanām 5-26
Shutting out external contacts, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, and evening out the in-breath and out-breath as they move within the nostrils…
sparśānkṛtvā bahirbāhyāṃścakṣuścaivāntare bhruvoḥ prāṇāpānau samau kṛtvā nāsābhyantaracāriṇau 5-27
…the sage who has mastered the senses, mind and intellect, whose highest aim is liberation, and who is free of longing, fear and anger, is truly free forever.
yatendriyamanobuddhirmunirmokṣaparāyaṇaḥ vigatecchābhayakrodho yaḥ sadā mukta eva saḥ 5-28
Knowing me as the one who receives all sacrifice and austerity, the great Lord of all the worlds and the friend of every being, one attains peace.
bhoktāraṃ yajñatapasāṃ sarvalokamaheśvaram suhṛdaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ jñātvā māṃ śāntimṛcchati 5-29
One who does the work that ought to be done without leaning on its fruits is both a renunciant and a yogi; not the one who has merely put out the sacred fire, nor the one who simply stops acting.
anāśritaḥ karmaphalaṃ kāryaṃ karma karoti yaḥ sa saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca na niragnirna cākriyaḥ 6-1
Know, Pandava, that what people call renunciation is in fact yoga, for no one becomes a yogi without first giving up self-willed intentions.
yaṃ saṃnyāsamiti prāhuryogaṃ taṃ viddhi pāṇḍava na hyasaṃnyastasaṃkalpo yogī bhavati kaścana 6-2
For the sage who wants to climb to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same person once established in yoga, calm is said to be the means.
ārurukṣormuneryogaṃ karma kāraṇamucyate yogārūḍhasya tasyaiva śamaḥ kāraṇamucyate 6-3
When a person no longer clings to the objects of the senses or to actions, and has let go of every self-willed intention, then he is called one who has mounted to yoga.
yadā hi nendriyārtheṣu na karmasvanuṣajjate sarvasaṃkalpasaṃnyāsī yogārūḍhastadocyate 6-4
Let a person raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is one's friend, and the self alone is one's enemy.
uddharedātmanātmānaṃ nātmānamavasādayet ātmaiva hyātmano bandhurātmaiva ripurātmanaḥ 6-5
The self is a friend to the one who has conquered himself by himself; but for one who has not mastered himself, that very self behaves with hostility, like an enemy.
bandhurātmātmanastasya yenātmaivātmanā jitaḥ anātmanastu śatrutve vartetātmaiva śatruvat 6-6
For one who has mastered himself and is deeply at peace, the supreme Self stays steady and collected amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour alike.
jitātmanaḥ praśāntasya paramātmā samāhitaḥ śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkheṣu tathā mānāpamānayoḥ 6-7

The yogi whose heart is content with knowledge and its lived realisation, who stands unshaken like an anvil, who has conquered the senses, and to whom a lump of earth, a stone and gold are all the same, is called truly joined in yoga.
jñānavijñānatṛptātmā kūṭastho vijitendriyaḥ yukta ityucyate yogī samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ 6-8
Still higher stands the one who looks with an even mind on well-wishers, friends and foes, the indifferent and the neutral, the hateful and kinsmen, and on the good and the wicked alike.
suhṛnmitrāryudāsīnamadhyasthadveṣyabandhuṣu sādhuṣvapi ca pāpeṣu samabuddhirviśiṣyate 6-9
A yogi should continually bring his mind to stillness, staying in a secluded place, alone, with mind and body restrained, free of cravings and without possessions.
yogī yuñjīta satatamātmānaṃ rahasi sthitaḥ ekākī yatacittātmā nirāśīraparigrahaḥ 6-10
In a clean place he should set up a firm seat for himself, neither too high nor too low, covered with kusha grass, then a deerskin, then a cloth.
śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiramāsanamātmanaḥ nātyucchritaṃ nātinīcaṃ cailājinakuśottaram 6-11
Seated there, making the mind one-pointed and keeping the workings of thought and senses in check, he should practise yoga to purify himself.
tatraikāgraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā yatacittendriyakriyaḥ upaviśyāsane yuñjyādyogamātmaviśuddhaye 6-12
Holding body, head and neck straight and motionless, staying steady, he should gaze at the tip of his own nose without looking about in any direction.
samaṃ kāyaśirogrīvaṃ dhārayannacalaṃ sthiraḥ samprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaścānavalokayan 6-13
Calm within, free of fear, firm in the vow of celibacy, restraining the mind and fixing his thought on me, he should sit joined in yoga, with me as his highest goal.
praśāntātmā vigatabhīrbrahmacārivrate sthitaḥ manaḥ saṃyamya maccitto yukta āsīta matparaḥ 6-14
Constantly uniting himself in this way, with his mind under control, the yogi reaches the peace that rests in me and culminates in nirvana.
yuñjannevaṃ sadātmānaṃ yogī niyatamānasaḥ śāntiṃ nirvāṇaparamāṃ matsaṃsthāmadhigacchati 6-15
Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, Arjuna; nor for one who sleeps too much, nor for one who stays awake too long.
nātyaśnatastu yogo'sti na caikāntamanaśnataḥ na cāti svapnaśīlasya jāgrato naiva cārjuna 6-16
For one who is measured in eating and recreation, measured in effort at work, and measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the remover of sorrow.
yuktāhāravihārasya yuktaceṣṭasya karmasu yuktasvapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkhahā 6-17
When the well-disciplined mind settles in the Self alone, free of longing for any object of desire, then a person is called united in yoga.
yadā viniyataṃ cittamātmanyevāvatiṣṭhate niḥspṛhaḥ sarvakāmebhyo yukta ityucyate tadā 6-18
"Like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker" — that is the image used for the yogi of controlled mind who practises union with the Self.
yathā dīpo nivātastho neṅgate sopamā smṛtā yogino yatacittasya yuñjato yogamātmanaḥ 6-19
That state where the mind, held in check by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and where, seeing the Self through the self, one is content in the Self...
yatroparamate cittaṃ niruddhaṃ yogasevayā yatra caivātmanātmānaṃ paśyannātmani tuṣyati 6-20
...where one knows that boundless happiness which the intellect can grasp but the senses cannot reach, and, established there, never strays from the truth...
sukhamātyantikaṃ yattad buddhigrāhyamatīndriyam vetti yatra na caivāyaṃ sthitaścalati tattvataḥ 6-21
...having gained which, one counts no other gain as greater, and settled in which, one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow...
yaṃ labdhvā cāparaṃ lābhaṃ manyate nādhikaṃ tataḥ yasminsthito na duḥkhena guruṇāpi vicālyate 6-22
...know that this is what is called yoga: the unlinking from all contact with sorrow. It should be practised with resolve and an undiscouraged heart.
taṃ vidyādduḥkhasaṃyogaviyogaṃ yogasaṃjñitam sa niścayena yoktavyo yogo'nirviṇṇacetasā 6-23
Giving up entirely all desires that spring from mental intention, and reining in the whole crowd of the senses from every side by the mind alone...
saṃkalpaprabhavānkāmāṃstyaktvā sarvānaśeṣataḥ manasaivendriyagrāmaṃ viniyamya samantataḥ 6-24
...one should gradually come to rest, with the intellect held firm by steadiness; fixing the mind in the Self, one should think of nothing else at all.
śanaiḥ śanairuparamedbuddhyā dhṛtigṛhītayā ātmasaṃsthaṃ manaḥ kṛtvā na kiṃcidapi cintayet 6-25
Whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, from there one should draw it back and bring it under control in the Self alone.
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet 6-26
Supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is fully calm, whose restless passion has subsided, who is free of taint and has become one with Brahman.
praśāntamanasaṃ hyenaṃ yoginaṃ sukhamuttamam upaiti śāntarajasaṃ brahmabhūtamakalmaṣam 6-27
Constantly joining himself in this way, the yogi, freed of impurity, easily enjoys the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
yuñjannevaṃ sadātmānaṃ yogī vigatakalmaṣaḥ sukhena brahmasaṃsparśamatyantaṃ sukhamaśnute 6-28
One whose self is joined in yoga sees the Self present in all beings and all beings in the Self, seeing the same everywhere.
sarvabhūtasthamātmānaṃ sarvabhūtāni cātmani īkṣate yogayuktātmā sarvatra samadarśanaḥ 6-29
Whoever sees me everywhere and sees everything in me — I am never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to me.
yo māṃ paśyati sarvatra sarvaṃ ca mayi paśyati tasyāhaṃ na praṇaśyāmi sa ca me na praṇaśyati 6-30
The yogi who, grounded in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all beings, lives in me, however he may be living.
sarvabhūtasthitaṃ yo māṃ bhajatyekatvamāsthitaḥ sarvathā vartamāno'pi sa yogī mayi vartate 6-31
Arjuna, the one who, by comparing others to himself, sees pleasure or pain everywhere as the same is regarded as the highest yogi.
ātmaupamyena sarvatra samaṃ paśyati yo'rjuna sukhaṃ vā yadi vā duḥkhaṃ sa yogī paramo mataḥ 6-32
Madhusudana, this yoga of evenness that you have taught — I do not see how it can stay firmly in place, because the mind is so restless.
arjuna uvāca yo'yaṃ yogastvayā proktaḥ sāmyena madhusūdana etasyāhaṃ na paśyāmi cañcalatvātsthitiṃ sthirām 6-33
For the mind is restless, Krishna — turbulent, strong and stubborn. Restraining it seems to me as hard as restraining the wind.
cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavaddṛḍham tasyāhaṃ nigrahaṃ manye vāyoriva suduṣkaram 6-34
There is no doubt, mighty-armed one, that the mind is unsteady and hard to rein in. Yet, son of Kunti, it can be held firm by persistent practice and by dispassion.
asaṃśayaṃ mahābāho mano durnigrahaṃ calam abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate 6-35
My view is that yoga is hard to attain for one who has not mastered himself; but one who has mastered himself and keeps striving can reach it by the right means.
asaṃyatātmanā yogo duṣprāpa iti me matiḥ vaśyātmanā tu yatatā śakyo'vāptumupāyataḥ 6-36
Krishna, what becomes of the person who has faith but lacks self-control, whose mind slips away from yoga, and who fails to reach its perfection?
arjuna uvāca ayatiḥ śraddhayopeto yogāccalitamānasaḥ aprāpya yogasaṃsiddhiṃ kāṃ gatiṃ kṛṣṇa gacchati 6-37
Mighty-armed one, having fallen from both, without a footing and bewildered on the path to Brahman, does he not perish like a scattered cloud?
kaccinnobhayavibhraṣṭaśchinnābhramiva naśyati apratiṣṭho mahābāho vimūḍho brahmaṇaḥ pathi 6-38
Krishna, please remove this doubt of mine completely; no one but you can dispel it.
etanme saṃśayaṃ kṛṣṇa chettumarhasyaśeṣataḥ tvadanyaḥ saṃśayasyāsya chettā na hyupapadyate 6-39
Partha, there is no ruin for him either in this world or the next; for, my friend, no one who does good ever comes to a bad end.
pārtha naiveha nāmutra vināśastasya vidyate na hi kalyāṇakṛtkaściddurgatiṃ tāta gacchati 6-40
One who has fallen from yoga reaches the worlds of the virtuous, lives there for many long years, and is then born into the home of pure and prosperous people.
prāpya puṇyakṛtāṃ lokānuṣitvā śāśvatīḥ samāḥ śucīnāṃ śrīmatāṃ gehe yogabhraṣṭo'bhijāyate 6-41
Or he is born into a family of wise yogis itself; but such a birth is very hard to come by in this world.
athavā yogināmeva kule bhavati dhīmatām etaddhi durlabhataraṃ loke janma yadīdṛśam 6-42
There he regains the understanding he had developed in his former body, and from that point, joy of the Kurus, he strives again, even harder, for perfection.
tatra taṃ buddhisaṃyogaṃ labhate paurvadehikam yatate ca tato bhūyaḥ saṃsiddhau kurunandana 6-43
By that earlier practice he is carried forward even without willing it; even one who merely seeks to know about yoga goes beyond the ritual word of the Vedas.
pūrvābhyāsena tenaiva hriyate hyavaśo'pi saḥ jijñāsurapi yogasya śabdabrahmātivartate 6-44
But the yogi who strives with diligence, cleansed of faults and brought to perfection over many births, then reaches the highest goal.
prayatnādyatamānastu yogī saṃśuddhakilbiṣaḥ anekajanmasaṃsiddhastato yāti parāṃ gatim 6-45
The yogi is greater than ascetics, considered greater even than scholars, and greater than those devoted to ritual works; therefore, Arjuna, be a yogi.
tapasvibhyo'dhiko yogī jñānibhyo'pi mato'dhikaḥ karmibhyaścādhiko yogī tasmādyogī bhavārjuna 6-46
And of all yogis, the one who, full of faith, worships me with his innermost self absorbed in me — that one I regard as the most closely united.
yogināmapi sarveṣāṃ madgatenāntarātmanā śraddhāvān bhajate yo māṃ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ 6-47
Listen, Partha, to how — with your mind attached to me, practising yoga and taking refuge in me — you will come to know me fully and without doubt.
mayyāsaktamanāḥ pārtha yogaṃ yuñjanmadāśrayaḥ asaṃśayaṃ samagraṃ māṃ yathā jñāsyasi tacchṛṇu 7-1
I will explain to you in full this knowledge together with its realisation; once you know it, nothing further remains to be known here.
jñānaṃ te'haṃ savijñānamidaṃ vakṣyāmyaśeṣataḥ yajjñātvā neha bhūyo'nyajjñātavyamavaśiṣyate 7-2
Among thousands of people, hardly one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and succeed, hardly one knows me as I truly am.
manuṣyāṇāṃ sahasreṣu kaścidyatati siddhaye yatatāmapi siddhānāṃ kaścinmāṃ vetti tattvataḥ 7-3
Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of 'I' — this is my nature, divided eightfold.
bhūmirāpo'nalo vāyuḥ khaṃ mano buddhireva ca ahaṃkāra itīyaṃ me bhinnā prakṛtiraṣṭadhā 7-4
This is my lower nature. But know, mighty-armed one, that beyond it I have another, higher nature — the living principle by which this world is upheld.
apareyamitastvanyāṃ prakṛtiṃ viddhi me parām jīvabhūtāṃ mahābāho yayedaṃ dhāryate jagat 7-5
Understand that all beings have these two as their source. I am the origin of the whole world and also its dissolution.
etadyonīni bhūtāni sarvāṇītyupadhāraya ahaṃ kṛtsnasya jagataḥ prabhavaḥ pralayastathā 7-6
Dhananjaya, there is nothing whatever higher than me. All this is strung on me, like a row of gems on a thread.
mattaḥ parataraṃ nānyatkiṃcidasti dhanaṃjaya mayi sarvamidaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva 7-7
Son of Kunti, I am the taste in water, the light in the moon and the sun, the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, and the vigour in human beings.
raso'hamapsu kaunteya prabhāsmi śaśisūryayoḥ praṇavaḥ sarvavedeṣu śabdaḥ khe pauruṣaṃ nṛṣu 7-8
I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in fire; I am the life in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
puṇyo gandhaḥ pṛthivyāṃ ca tejaścāsmi vibhāvasau jīvanaṃ sarvabhūteṣu tapaścāsmi tapasviṣu 7-9
Partha, know me as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent and the splendour of the splendid.
bījaṃ māṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ viddhi pārtha sanātanam buddhirbuddhimatāmasmi tejastejasvināmaham 7-10
In the strong I am strength free of craving and attachment; and in beings, best of the Bharatas, I am desire that does not go against dharma.
balaṃ balavatāṃ cāhaṃ kāmarāgavivarjitam dharmāviruddho bhūteṣu kāmo'smi bharatarṣabha 7-11
Whatever states of being there are — sattvic, rajasic or tamasic — know that they come from me alone. Yet I am not in them; they are in me.
ye caiva sāttvikā bhāvā rājasāstāmasāśca ye matta eveti tānviddhi na tvahaṃ teṣu te mayi 7-12
Deluded by these states made of the three gunas, this whole world fails to recognise me, who stand beyond them, imperishable.
tribhirguṇamayairbhāvairebhiḥ sarvamidaṃ jagat mohitaṃ nābhijānāti māmebhyaḥ paramavyayam 7-13
This divine maya of mine, made of the gunas, is very hard to get past; but those who take refuge in me alone cross beyond it.
daivī hyeṣā guṇamayī mama māyā duratyayā māmeva ye prapadyante māyāmetāṃ taranti te 7-14
Evildoers, the deluded and the lowest of people do not turn to me — their understanding stolen by maya, they have taken on a demonic disposition.
na māṃ duṣkṛtino mūḍhāḥ prapadyante narādhamāḥ māyayāpahṛtajñānā āsuraṃ bhāvamāśritāḥ 7-15
Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.
caturvidhā bhajante māṃ janāḥ sukṛtino'rjuna ārto jijñāsurarthārthī jñānī ca bharatarṣabha 7-16
Of these the wise one, ever united and devoted to the One alone, stands out. For I am exceedingly dear to the wise, and the wise one is dear to me.
teṣāṃ jñānī nityayukta ekabhaktirviśiṣyate priyo hi jñānino'tyarthamahaṃ sa ca mama priyaḥ 7-17
All of these are noble, but the wise one I consider my very Self; for, steadfast in mind, he is anchored in me alone as the highest goal.
udārāḥ sarva evaite jñānī tvātmaiva me matam āsthitaḥ sa hi yuktātmā māmevānuttamāṃ gatim 7-18
Only after many births does the one who truly knows take refuge in me, seeing that Vasudeva is all there is. A great soul like that is hard indeed to find.
bahūnāṃ janmanāmante jñānavānmāṃ prapadyate vāsudevaḥ sarvamiti sa mahātmā sudurlabhaḥ 7-19
Those whose understanding has been carried off by this or that desire turn to other gods, following one observance or another, driven by their own nature.
kāmaistaistairhṛtajñānāḥ prapadyante'nyadevatāḥ taṃ taṃ niyamamāsthāya prakṛtyā niyatāḥ svayā 7-20
Whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his unwavering.
yo yo yāṃ yāṃ tanuṃ bhaktaḥ śraddhayārcitumicchati tasya tasyācalāṃ śraddhāṃ tāmeva vidadhāmyaham 7-21
Endowed with that faith he seeks to worship that form, and from it he obtains his desires — yet those are in truth granted by me alone.
sa tayā śraddhayā yuktastasyārādhanamīhate labhate ca tataḥ kāmānmayaiva vihitānhi tān 7-22
But the fruit gained by those of small understanding is perishable. Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
antavattu phalaṃ teṣāṃ tadbhavatyalpamedhasām devāndevayajo yānti madbhaktā yānti māmapi 7-23
The undiscerning think of me, the unmanifest, as having taken on a manifest form, not knowing my higher being, which is imperishable and unsurpassed.
avyaktaṃ vyaktimāpannaṃ manyante māmabuddhayaḥ paraṃ bhāvamajānanto mamāvyayamanuttamam 7-24
Veiled by my yogamaya, I am not revealed to everyone. This deluded world does not recognise me as unborn and imperishable.
nāhaṃ prakāśaḥ sarvasya yogamāyāsamāvṛtaḥ mūḍho'yaṃ nābhijānāti loko māmajamavyayam 7-25
Arjuna, I know the beings of the past, the present and the future; but no one knows me.
vedāhaṃ samatītāni vartamānāni cārjuna bhaviṣyāṇi ca bhūtāni māṃ tu veda na kaścana 7-26
Through the delusion of opposites that arises from liking and aversion, Bharata, all beings fall into bewilderment at birth, scorcher of foes.
icchādveṣasamutthena dvandvamohena bhārata sarvabhūtāni saṃmohaṃ sarge yānti parantapa 7-27
But people of virtuous deeds whose wrongdoing has come to an end are freed from the delusion of opposites and worship me with firm resolve.
yeṣāṃ tvantagataṃ pāpaṃ janānāṃ puṇyakarmaṇām te dvandvamohanirmuktā bhajante māṃ dṛḍhavratāḥ 7-28
Those who take refuge in me and strive for release from old age and death come to know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self, and all action.
jarāmaraṇamokṣāya māmāśritya yatanti ye te brahma tadviduḥ kṛtsnamadhyātmaṃ karma cākhilam 7-29
Those who know me together with the physical realm, the divine realm and the lord of sacrifice — they, with minds steadfast, know me even at the moment of departure.
sādhibhūtādhidaivaṃ māṃ sādhiyajñaṃ ca ye viduḥ prayāṇakāle'pi ca māṃ te viduryuktacetasaḥ 7-30
Purushottama, what is that Brahman? What is the inner self? What is action? What is called the physical realm, and what is said to be the divine realm?
arjuna uvāca kiṃ tadbrahma kimadhyātmaṃ kiṃ karma puruṣottama adhibhūtaṃ ca kiṃ proktamadhidaivaṃ kimucyate 8-1
Madhusudana, who is the lord of sacrifice here in this body, and how? And how are you to be known at the time of death by those who have mastered themselves?
adhiyajñaḥ kathaṃ ko'tra dehe'sminmadhusūdana prayāṇakāle ca kathaṃ jñeyo'si niyatātmabhiḥ 8-2
Brahman is the imperishable, the supreme. Its presence as one's own being is called the inner self. The creative outpouring that brings beings into existence is called action.
akṣaraṃ brahma paramaṃ svabhāvo'dhyātmamucyate bhūtabhāvodbhavakaro visargaḥ karmasaṃjñitaḥ 8-3
The physical realm is perishable existence; the divine realm is the cosmic Person; and the lord of sacrifice, best of the embodied, is I myself, here in this body.
adhibhūtaṃ kṣaro bhāvaḥ puruṣaścādhidaivatam adhiyajño'hamevātra dehe dehabhṛtāṃ vara 8-4
Whoever leaves the body at the time of death remembering me alone attains my being; of this there is no doubt.
antakāle ca māmeva smaranmuktvā kalevaram yaḥ prayāti sa madbhāvaṃ yāti nāstyatra saṃśayaḥ 8-5
Whatever state of being a person remembers when finally giving up the body, son of Kunti, to that very state he goes, having always been shaped by it.
yaṃ yaṃ vāpi smaranbhāvaṃ tyajatyante kalevaram taṃ tamevaiti kaunteya sadā tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ 8-6
So at all times remember me, and fight. With mind and intellect offered to me, you will surely come to me.
tasmātsarveṣu kāleṣu māmanusmara yudhya ca mayyarpitamanobuddhirmāmevaiṣyasyasaṃśayaḥ 8-7
With a mind trained by the yoga of practice and straying nowhere else, contemplating constantly, Partha, one reaches the supreme divine Person.
abhyāsayogayuktena cetasā nānyagāminā paramaṃ puruṣaṃ divyaṃ yāti pārthānucintayan 8-8
One who meditates on the seer, the ancient one, the ruler, subtler than the subtlest, the sustainer of all, of inconceivable form, radiant as the sun and beyond all darkness...
kaviṃ purāṇamanuśāsitāramaṇoraṇīyāṃsamanusmaredyaḥ sarvasya dhātāramacintyarūpamādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt 8-9
...at the time of departure, with an unwavering mind, filled with devotion and by the strength of yoga, drawing the life-breath fully between the eyebrows — he reaches that supreme divine Person.
prayāṇakāle manasācalena bhaktyā yukto yogabalena caiva bhruvormadhye prāṇamāveśya samyak sa taṃ paraṃ puruṣamupaiti divyam 8-10
That which knowers of the Veda call imperishable, which ascetics free of passion enter, and in search of which people live a life of celibacy — that goal I will describe to you briefly.
yadakṣaraṃ vedavido vadanti viśanti yadyatayo vītarāgāḥ yadicchanto brahmacaryaṃ caranti tatte padaṃ saṃgraheṇa pravakṣye 8-11
Closing all the gates of the body, confining the mind in the heart, placing his life-breath at the crown of the head, and holding firm in yogic concentration...
