You are tied to nothing at all. Being pure, what would you renounce? Letting this bundle of body and mind fall apart, just so, let yourself dissolve.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca na te saṃgo'sti kenāpi kiṃ śuddhastyaktumicchasi saṃghātavilayaṃ kurvannevameva layaṃ vraja 5-1
The universe rises from you like a bubble from the sea. Knowing the Self to be one, just so, let yourself dissolve.
udeti bhavato viśvaṃ vāridheriva budbudaḥ iti jñātvaikamātmānaṃ evameva layaṃ vraja 5-2
Though it is right before your eyes, the universe has no real substance, and so it does not exist in you, the stainless one, any more than the snake in a rope. Just so, let yourself dissolve.
pratyakṣamapyavastutvād viśvaṃ nāstyamale tvayi rajjusarpa iva vyaktaṃ evameva layaṃ vraja 5-3
Same in pain and pleasure, full, equal in hope and despair, equal in life and death — being so, just so, let yourself dissolve.
samaduḥkhasukhaḥ pūrṇa āśānairāśyayoḥ samaḥ samajīvitamṛtyuḥ sannevameva layaṃ vraja 5-4
I am boundless like space; the world of nature is like a pot. This is knowledge, and so there is nothing to give up, nothing to take hold of, nothing to dissolve.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca ākāśavadananto'haṃ ghaṭavat prākṛtaṃ jagat iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ 6-1
I am like the great ocean; this spread of the world is like its waves. This is knowledge, and so there is nothing to give up, nothing to take hold of, nothing to dissolve.
mahodadhirivāhaṃ sa prapaṃco vīcisa'nnibhaḥ iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ 6-2
I am like the mother-of-pearl; the imagined universe is like the silver seen in it. This is knowledge, and so there is nothing to give up, nothing to take hold of, nothing to dissolve.
ahaṃ sa śuktisaṅkāśo rūpyavad viśvakalpanā iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ 6-3
I am in all beings, and all beings are in me. This is knowledge, and so there is nothing to give up, nothing to take hold of, nothing to dissolve.
ahaṃ vā sarvabhūteṣu sarvabhūtānyatho mayi iti jñānaṃ tathaitasya na tyāgo na graho layaḥ 6-4
In me, the boundless ocean, the ship of the world drifts here and there, driven by its own wind. I am not troubled by it.
janaka uvāca mayyanaṃtamahāṃbhodhau viśvapota itastataḥ bhramati svāṃtavātena na mamāstyasahiṣṇutā 7-1
In me, the boundless ocean, the waves of the world rise or sink by their own nature. Let them rise or vanish; I neither grow nor shrink.
mayyanaṃtamahāṃbhodhau jagadvīciḥ svabhāvataḥ udetu vāstamāyātu na me vṛddhirna ca kṣatiḥ 7-2
In me, the boundless ocean, the universe is only an imagining. Utterly still and without form, in this alone I abide.
mayyanaṃtamahāṃbhodhau viśvaṃ nāma vikalpanā atiśāṃto nirākāra etadevāhamāsthitaḥ 7-3
The Self is not in things, nor are things in that boundless, spotless one. So, unattached, wanting nothing and at peace, in this alone I abide.
nātmā bhāveṣu no bhāvastatrānante niraṃjane ityasakto'spṛhaḥ śānta etadevāhamāstitaḥ 7-4
Ah, I am pure consciousness alone, and the world is like a magician's show. So how, and where, could the idea of rejecting or accepting anything arise for me?
aho cinmātramevāhaṃ indrajālopamaṃ jagat ato mama kathaṃ kutra heyopādeyakalpanā 7-5
It is bondage when the mind wants something or grieves over something, lets go of something or grabs something, is pleased by something or angered by something.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca tadā bandho yadā cittaṃ kiṃcid vāṃchati śocati kiṃcin muṃcati gṛṇhāti kiṃciddhṛṣyati kupyati 8-1
It is liberation when the mind does not want or grieve, does not let go or grab, is not pleased or angered.
tadā muktiryadā cittaṃ na vāṃchati na śocati na muṃcati na gṛṇhāti na hṛṣyati na kupyati 8-2
It is bondage when the mind clings to any of the things it sees. It is liberation when the mind clings to nothing it sees.
tadā bandho yadā cittaṃ saktaṃ kāsvapi dṛṣṭiṣu tadā mokṣo yadā cittamasaktaṃ sarvadṛṣṭiṣu 8-3
When there is no 'I', there is liberation; when there is 'I', there is bondage. Seeing this, lightly and without effort, neither take hold of anything nor push anything away.
yadā nāhaṃ tadā mokṣo yadāhaṃ bandhanaṃ tadā matveti helayā kiṃcinmā gṛhāṇa vimuṃca mā 8-4
Things done and not done, and the pairs of opposites — when have they ever ended, and for whom? Knowing this, be dispassionate here, given to letting go and bound by no vows.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca kṛtākṛte ca dvandvāni kadā śāntāni kasya vā evaṃ jñātveha nirvedād bhava tyāgaparo'vratī 9-1
Child, only some rare blessed one, by watching how people strive, has lost the wish to live, the hunger to enjoy, and the urge to know.
kasyāpi tāta dhanyasya lokaceṣṭāvalokanāt jīvitecchā bubhukṣā ca bubhutsopaśamaḥ gatāḥ 9-2
Having seen for certain that all this is fleeting, spoiled by the three kinds of suffering, hollow, contemptible and fit to be left, one becomes calm.
anityaṃ sarvamevedaṃ tāpatritayadūṣitam asāraṃ ninditaṃ heyamiti niścitya śāmyati 9-3
What time or what age of life is there when people are free of the pairs of opposites? Ignoring them and living with whatever comes, one reaches fulfilment.
ko'sau kālo vayaḥ kiṃ vā yatra dvandvāni no nṛṇāṃ tānyupekṣya yathāprāptavartī siddhimavāpnuyāt 9-4
Seeing how the great sages, the saints and the yogis all hold different views, what person would not grow weary of it all and become calm?
nānā mataṃ maharṣīṇāṃ sādhūnāṃ yogināṃ tathā dṛṣṭvā nirvedamāpannaḥ ko na śāmyati mānavaḥ 9-5
Is he not a true guru who has fully known the nature of consciousness, and who, through dispassion, evenness and right reasoning, carries one across the round of birth and death?
kṛtvā mūrtiparijñānaṃ caitanyasya na kiṃ guruḥ nirvedasamatāyuktyā yastārayati saṃsṛteḥ 9-6
See the changes of the elements as they truly are, as nothing but the elements. In that very moment you will be free of bondage and rest in your own nature.
paśya bhūtavikārāṃstvaṃ bhūtamātrān yathārthataḥ tatkṣaṇād bandhanirmuktaḥ svarūpastho bhaviṣyasi 9-7
Latent desires are themselves the world of becoming, so let go of them all. Dropping them is dropping the world; then remain, from now on, however you happen to be.
vāsanā eva saṃsāra iti sarvā vimuṃca tāḥ tattyāgo vāsanātyāgātsthitiradya yathā tathā 9-8
Put away desire, which is your enemy, and wealth, which is full of trouble, and even duty, which is the root of both. Be indifferent to all of them.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca vihāya vairiṇaṃ kāmamarthaṃ cānarthasaṃkulaṃ dharmamapyetayorhetuṃ sarvatrānādaraṃ kuru 10-1
See friends, lands, money, houses, wives, inheritances and all such riches as a dream or a magic show, lasting three days or five.
svapnendrajālavat paśya dināni trīṇi paṃca vā mitrakṣetradhanāgāradāradāyādisaṃpadaḥ 10-2
Wherever there is craving, know that the world of becoming is right there. Taking firm hold of mature dispassion, be free of craving and be happy.
yatra yatra bhavettṛṣṇā saṃsāraṃ viddhi tatra vai prauḍhavairāgyamāśritya vītatṛṣṇaḥ sukhī bhava 10-3
Bondage is made of craving alone, and its ending is called liberation. Simply by not clinging to the world, one finds contentment again and again.
tṛṣṇāmātrātmako bandhastannāśo mokṣa ucyate bhavāsaṃsaktimātreṇa prāptituṣṭirmuhurmuhuḥ 10-4
You are the one pure consciousness; the world is inert and unreal. Even ignorance is nothing at all. So what is left for you to want to know?
tvamekaścetanaḥ śuddho jaḍaṃ viśvamasattathā avidyāpi na kiṃcitsā kā bubhutsā tathāpi te 10-5
Kingdoms, sons, wives, bodies and pleasures have been lost to you birth after birth, even though you clung to them.
rājyaṃ sutāḥ kalatrāṇi śarīrāṇi sukhāni ca saṃsaktasyāpi naṣṭāni tava janmani janmani 10-6
Enough of wealth, of pleasure, and even of good deeds. In the wilderness of the world, the mind never found rest through any of them.
alamarthena kāmena sukṛtenāpi karmaṇā ebhyaḥ saṃsārakāntāre na viśrāntamabhūn manaḥ 10-7
For how many lives have you not toiled with body, mind and speech at painful, exhausting work? At least now, let it come to rest.
kṛtaṃ na kati janmāni kāyena manasā girā duḥkhamāyāsadaṃ karma tadadyāpyuparamyatām 10-8
One who knows for certain that existence, non-existence and change all arise from the nature of things becomes free of change and distress, and easily finds peace.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca bhāvābhāvavikāraśca svabhāvāditi niścayī nirvikāro gatakleśaḥ sukhenaivopaśāmyati 11-1
One who knows for certain that God is the maker of everything and there is no other here has all his hopes melted away within; at peace, he clings to nothing anywhere.
īśvaraḥ sarvanirmātā nehānya iti niścayī antargalitasarvāśaḥ śāntaḥ kvāpi na sajjate 11-2
One who knows for certain that misfortune and good fortune come in their time by destiny alone stays content, his senses at rest; he neither longs nor grieves.
āpadaḥ saṃpadaḥ kāle daivādeveti niścayī tṛptaḥ svasthendriyo nityaṃ na vānchati na śocati 11-3
One who knows for certain that pleasure and pain, birth and death come by destiny alone sees nothing to be achieved and makes no strain; even while acting he is not stained.
sukhaduḥkhe janmamṛtyū daivādeveti niścayī sādhyādarśī nirāyāsaḥ kurvannapi na lipyate 11-4
One who knows for certain that suffering in this world comes from anxious thinking and nothing else is freed of it — happy, at peace, his wants fallen away everywhere.
cintayā jāyate duḥkhaṃ nānyatheheti niścayī tayā hīnaḥ sukhī śāntaḥ sarvatra galitaspṛhaḥ 11-5
One who knows for certain, 'I am not the body, the body is not mine, I am awareness,' is as if he has reached absolute aloneness; he does not recall what was done or left undone.
nāhaṃ deho na me deho bodho'hamiti niścayī kaivalyaṃ iva saṃprāpto na smaratyakṛtaṃ kṛtam 11-6
One who knows for certain, 'From Brahma down to a blade of grass, it is all I alone,' is free of thought, pure and at peace, untroubled by what is gained or not gained.
ābrahmastaṃbaparyantaṃ ahameveti niścayī nirvikalpaḥ śuciḥ śāntaḥ prāptāprāptavinirvṛtaḥ 11-7
One who knows for certain that this universe, with all its many wonders, is nothing at all becomes free of latent desires; pure shining awareness, he rests in peace as if nothing were there.
nānāścaryamidaṃ viśvaṃ na kiṃciditi niścayī nirvāsanaḥ sphūrtimātro na kiṃcidiva śāmyati 11-8
First I lost patience with the work of the body, then with long talk, and then with thinking itself; and so I remain just as I am.
janaka uvāca kāyakṛtyāsahaḥ pūrvaṃ tato vāgvistarāsahaḥ atha cintāsahastasmād evamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-1
Since I take no delight in sound and the other objects, and since the Self is never something seen, my heart is free of scattering and rests one-pointed; and so I remain just as I am.
prītyabhāvena śabdāderadṛśyatvena cātmanaḥ vikṣepaikāgrahṛdaya evamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-2
Scattering comes from false superimposition and the like, and so one takes up practice for samadhi. Seeing this pattern, I remain just as I am.
samādhyāsādivikṣiptau vyavahāraḥ samādhaye evaṃ vilokya niyamaṃ evamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-3
Having nothing to reject or accept, and so no joy or sorrow, today, O brahmin, I remain just as I am.
heyopādeyavirahād evaṃ harṣaviṣādayoḥ abhāvādadya he brahmann evamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-4
Stages of life or none at all, meditation, renouncing what the mind clings to — seeing that through these only my own mental fancies arise, I remain just as I am.
āśramānāśramaṃ dhyānaṃ cittasvīkṛtavarjanaṃ vikalpaṃ mama vīkṣyaitairevamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-5
Doing actions springs from ignorance, and so does ceasing from them. Understanding this truth fully, I remain just as I am.
karmānuṣṭhānamajñānād yathaivoparamastathā buddhvā samyagidaṃ tattvaṃ evamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-6
Even when thinking of the unthinkable, one still takes on the form of thought. So, giving up even that contemplation, I remain just as I am.
aciṃtyaṃ ciṃtyamāno'pi cintārūpaṃ bhajatyasau tyaktvā tadbhāvanaṃ tasmād evamevāhamāsthitaḥ 12-7
Whoever has done just this has fulfilled the purpose of life. Whoever is just so by nature has fulfilled the purpose of life.
evameva kṛtaṃ yena sa kṛtārtho bhavedasau evameva svabhāvo yaḥ sa kṛtārtho bhavedasau 12-8
The ease that comes from owning nothing is hard to find even for one who wears only a loincloth. So, letting go of both giving up and taking, I live at ease, as it suits me.
janaka uvāca akiṃcanabhavaṃ svāsthyaṃ kaupīnatve'pi durlabhaṃ tyāgādāne vihāyāsmādahamāse yathāsukham 13-1
Somewhere the body gets weary, somewhere the tongue gets tired, somewhere the mind. Leaving all that behind, I rest happily in life's true aim.
kutrāpi khedaḥ kāyasya jihvā kutrāpi khidyate manaḥ kutrāpi tattyaktvā puruṣārthe sthitaḥ sukham 13-2
Seeing truly that nothing is ever really done, I do whatever comes to be done when it comes, and live at ease, as it suits me.
kṛtaṃ kimapi naiva syād iti saṃcintya tattvataḥ yadā yatkartumāyāti tat kṛtvāse yathāsukham 13-3
Yogis who identify with the body insist on action or on inaction. Free of both union and separation, I live at ease, as it suits me.
karmanaiṣkarmyanirbandhabhāvā dehasthayoginaḥ saṃyogāyogavirahādahamāse yathāsukham 13-4
I gain nothing and lose nothing by standing, walking or lying down; so whether I stand, walk or sleep, I live at ease, as it suits me.
arthānarthau na me sthityā gatyā na śayanena vā tiṣṭhan gacchan svapan tasmādahamāse yathāsukham 13-5
I lose nothing by sleeping and gain nothing by striving. So, letting go of both loss and elation, I live at ease, as it suits me.
svapato nāsti me hāniḥ siddhiryatnavato na vā nāśollāsau vihāyāsmādahamāse yathāsukham 13-6
Having seen again and again how pleasure and the like come and go without any rule among things, I let go of good and bad, and live at ease, as it suits me.
sukhādirūpā niyamaṃ bhāveṣvālokya bhūriśaḥ śubhāśubhe vihāyāsmādahamāse yathāsukham 13-7
One whose mind is by nature empty, who thinks of things only by oversight, who is as if awake even in sleep — his memories of worldly life have worn away.
janaka uvāca prakṛtyā śūnyacitto yaḥ pramādād bhāvabhāvanaḥ nidrito bodhita iva kṣīṇasaṃsmaraṇo hi saḥ 14-1
Where now is wealth, where are friends, where are the thieves that are my senses' objects? Where is scripture, where is knowledge, now that my wanting has melted away?
kva dhanāni kva mitrāṇi kva me viṣayadasyavaḥ kva śāstraṃ kva ca vijñānaṃ yadā me galitā spṛhā 14-2
Now that I have known the witness, the supreme Self and the Lord, and expect nothing from either bondage or freedom, I have no worry about liberation.
vijñāte sākṣipuruṣe paramātmani ceśvare nairāśye baṃdhamokṣe ca na ciṃtā muktaye mama 14-3
He is empty of thoughts within and moves freely without, seeming like someone confused; only those like him can know the states he passes through.
aṃtarvikalpaśūnyasya bahiḥ svacchandacāriṇaḥ bhrāntasyeva daśāstāstāstādṛśā eva jānate 14-4
A person of pure understanding reaches life's goal even from a passing word of instruction, while another may keep inquiring all his life and still stay confused about it.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca yathātathopadeśena kṛtārthaḥ sattvabuddhimān ājīvamapi jijñāsuḥ parastatra vimuhyati 15-1
Liberation is losing the taste for sense objects; bondage is relishing them. That is all there is to know. Now do as you wish.
mokṣo viṣayavairasyaṃ bandho vaiṣayiko rasaḥ etāvadeva vijñānaṃ yathecchasi tathā kuru 15-2
This knowledge of truth turns an eloquent, clever, hard-striving person into one who is silent, still and idle. That is why those hungry for enjoyment avoid it.
vāgmiprājñamahodyogaṃ janaṃ mūkajaḍālasaṃ karoti tattvabodho'yamatastyakto bubhukṣubhiḥ 15-3
You are not the body, nor is the body yours; you are neither the doer nor the enjoyer. You are consciousness itself, ever the witness, needing nothing. Go about happily.
na tvaṃ deho na te deho bhoktā kartā na vā bhavān cidrūpo'si sadā sākṣī nirapekṣaḥ sukhaṃ cara 15-4
Attraction and aversion belong to the mind, and the mind is never yours. You are free of thought, pure awareness, unchanging. Go about happily.
rāgadveṣau manodharmau na manaste kadācana nirvikalpo'si bodhātmā nirvikāraḥ sukhaṃ cara 15-5
Knowing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, be free of 'I' and 'mine', and be happy.
sarvabhūteṣu cātmānaṃ sarvabhūtāni cātmani vijñāya nirahaṃkāro nirmamastvaṃ sukhī bhava 15-6
That in which this world shimmers like waves on the sea, that is what you are, without doubt. You who are consciousness itself, let the fever go.
viśvaṃ sphurati yatredaṃ taraṃgā iva sāgare tattvameva na sandehaścinmūrte vijvaro bhava 15-7
Have faith, child, have faith; do not be confused about this, my dear. You are the Self, knowledge itself, the Lord, beyond nature (prakriti).
śraddhatsva tāta śraddhatsva nātra mohaṃ kuruṣva bhoḥ jñānasvarūpo bhagavānātmā tvaṃ prakṛteḥ paraḥ 15-8
The body, wrapped in the qualities (gunas), stays, comes and goes. The Self neither goes nor comes. Why grieve over it?
guṇaiḥ saṃveṣṭito dehastiṣṭhatyāyāti yāti ca ātmā na gaṃtā nāgaṃtā kimenamanuśocasi 15-9
Let the body last until the end of the age, or let it go this very day. What gain or loss is there for you, who are pure consciousness?
dehastiṣṭhatu kalpāntaṃ gacchatvadyaiva vā punaḥ kva vṛddhiḥ kva ca vā hānistava cinmātrarūpiṇaḥ 15-10
In you, the endless great ocean, let the wave of the world rise or fall by its own nature. You neither gain nor lose.
tvayyanaṃtamahāṃbhodhau viśvavīciḥ svabhāvataḥ udetu vāstamāyātu na te vṛddhirna vā kṣatiḥ 15-11
Child, you are pure consciousness; this world is not separate from you. So who could reject or accept anything, and how, and where?
tāta cinmātrarūpo'si na te bhinnamidaṃ jagat ataḥ kasya kathaṃ kutra heyopādeyakalpanā 15-12
In you, the one, the imperishable, the peaceful, the stainless sky of consciousness, where is birth, where is action, where is even the ego?
ekasminnavyaye śānte cidākāśe'male tvayi kuto janma kutaḥ karma kuto'haṃkāra eva ca 15-13
Whatever you see, it is you alone appearing there. Do bracelets, armlets and anklets shine apart from the gold?
yattvaṃ paśyasi tatraikastvameva pratibhāsase kiṃ pṛthak bhāsate svarṇāt kaṭakāṃgadanūpuram 15-14
Give up dividing things into 'this I am' and 'this I am not'. Knowing for certain that all is the Self, let go of intentions and be happy.
ayaṃ so'hamayaṃ nāhaṃ vibhāgamiti saṃtyaja sarvamātmeti niścitya niḥsaṅkalpaḥ sukhī bhava 15-15
The world exists only through your own ignorance; in truth you alone are. Apart from you there is no one, bound to worldly life or free of it.
tavaivājñānato viśvaṃ tvamekaḥ paramārthataḥ tvatto'nyo nāsti saṃsārī nāsaṃsārī ca kaścana 15-16
One who knows for certain that this world is mere illusion and nothing at all is freed of latent desires; he is sheer radiance and comes to rest as though he were nothing.
bhrāntimātramidaṃ viśvaṃ na kiṃciditi niścayī nirvāsanaḥ sphūrtimātro na kiṃcidiva śāmyati 15-17
In the ocean of existence there was, is and will be only one. You have no bondage and no liberation. Your work is done; go about happily.
eka eva bhavāṃbhodhāvāsīdasti bhaviṣyati na te bandho'sti mokṣo vā kṛtakṛtyaḥ sukhaṃ cara 15-18
You who are made of consciousness, do not stir up your mind with wanting and doubting. Grow calm and rest happily in your own Self, which is bliss itself.
mā saṅkalpavikalpābhyāṃ cittaṃ kṣobhaya cinmaya upaśāmya sukhaṃ tiṣṭha svātmanyānandavigrahe 15-19
Give up meditation altogether; hold nothing in your heart. You are the Self, already free. What will you achieve by pondering?
tyajaiva dhyānaṃ sarvatra mā kiṃciddhṛdi dhāraya ātmā tvaṃ mukta evāsi kiṃ vimṛśya kariṣyasi 15-20
You may recite or listen to many scriptures again and again, child, yet you will not rest in yourself until you forget everything.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca ācakṣva śṛṇu vā tāta nānāśāstrāṇyanekaśaḥ tathāpi na tava svāsthyaṃ sarvavismaraṇād ṛte 16-1
Enjoy pleasures, do your work, or practise samadhi, knowing one; still, your mind will long above all for the state where every hope has fallen away.
bhogaṃ karma samādhiṃ vā kuru vijña tathāpi te cittaṃ nirastasarvāśamatyarthaṃ rocayiṣyati 16-2
Everyone is miserable because of effort, yet no one understands this. Through this one teaching alone, the fortunate one reaches release.
āyāsātsakalo duḥkhī nainaṃ jānāti kaścana anenaivopadeśena dhanyaḥ prāpnoti nirvṛtim 16-3
Happiness belongs to that master of idleness who finds even opening and closing his eyes a bother, and to no one else.
vyāpāre khidyate yastu nimeṣonmeṣayorapi tasyālasya dhurīṇasya sukhaṃ nānyasya kasyacit 16-4
When the mind is free of opposites like 'this is done, this is not done', it no longer cares for duty, wealth, pleasure or liberation.
idaṃ kṛtamidaṃ neti dvaṃdvairmuktaṃ yadā manaḥ dharmārthakāmamokṣeṣu nirapekṣaṃ tadā bhavet 16-5
The renunciant hates sense objects; the passionate person is greedy for them. But one who neither grasps nor lets go is neither renunciant nor passionate.
virakto viṣayadveṣṭā rāgī viṣayalolupaḥ grahamokṣavihīnastu na virakto na rāgavān 16-6
As long as craving lives, the soil in which want of discernment grows, so long will the sense of rejecting and accepting remain, the sprout of the tree of worldly life.
heyopādeyatā tāvatsaṃsāraviṭapāṃkuraḥ spṛhā jīvati yāvad vai nirvicāradaśāspadam 16-7
Activity breeds attachment, and withdrawal breeds aversion. The wise person, free of opposites like a child, simply stays as he is.
pravṛttau jāyate rāgo nirvṛttau dveṣa eva hi nirdvandvo bālavad dhīmān evameva vyavasthitaḥ 16-8
The passionate person wants to leave worldly life to escape sorrow. But one free of passion is free of sorrow and is not troubled even while in the world.
hātumicchati saṃsāraṃ rāgī duḥkhajihāsayā vītarāgo hi nirduḥkhastasminnapi na khidyati 16-9
One who takes pride even in liberation and still claims the body as his own is neither a knower nor a yogi; he simply has his share of suffering.
yasyābhimāno mokṣe'pi dehe'pi mamatā tathā na ca jñānī na vā yogī kevalaṃ duḥkhabhāgasau 16-10
Even if Shiva, Vishnu or lotus-born Brahma were your teacher, you would not rest in yourself until you forget everything.
haro yadyupadeṣṭā te hariḥ kamalajo'pi vā tathāpi na tava svāsthyaṃ sarvavismaraṇādṛte 16-11
One who is content, with senses clear, and always delights in being alone, has won the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of yoga practice as well.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca tena jñānaphalaṃ prāptaṃ yogābhyāsaphalaṃ tathā tṛptaḥ svacchendriyo nityaṃ ekākī ramate tu yaḥ 17-1
Ah, the knower of truth is never troubled in this world, for he alone fills this whole sphere of the universe.
na kadācijjagatyasmin tattvajño hanta khidyati yata ekena tenedaṃ pūrṇaṃ brahmāṇḍamaṇḍalam 17-2
No sense objects ever delight one who rejoices in the Self, just as neem leaves do not please an elephant that loves sallaki leaves.
na jātu viṣayāḥ ke'pi svārāmaṃ harṣayantyamī sallakīpallavaprītamivebhaṃ niṃbapallavāḥ 17-3
One who does not cling to pleasures already enjoyed and does not crave those not yet enjoyed is rare in this world.
yastu bhogeṣu bhukteṣu na bhavatyadhivāsitaḥ abhukteṣu nirākāṃkṣī tādṛśo bhavadurlabhaḥ 17-4
In this world we see people hungry for enjoyment and people hungry for liberation, but rare indeed is the great-souled one who wants neither.
bubhukṣuriha saṃsāre mumukṣurapi dṛśyate bhogamokṣanirākāṃkṣī viralo hi mahāśayaḥ 17-5
Only a rare, open-hearted person has no sense of rejecting or accepting duty, wealth, pleasure, liberation, life or death.
dharmārthakāmamokṣeṣu jīvite maraṇe tathā kasyāpyudāracittasya heyopādeyatā na hi 17-6
He neither wishes for the world to dissolve nor resents its going on. So the blessed one lives happily on whatever livelihood comes.
vāṃchā na viśvavilaye na dveṣastasya ca sthitau yathā jīvikayā tasmād dhanya āste yathā sukham 17-7
Fulfilled by this knowledge, his thinking mind dissolved, the accomplished one lives happily, seeing, hearing, touching, smelling and eating.
kṛtārtho'nena jñānenetyevaṃ galitadhīḥ kṛtī paśyan śṛṇvan spṛśan jighrann aśnannaste yathā sukham 17-8
For one in whom the ocean of worldly life has dried up, the gaze is empty, actions have no purpose, the senses are idle; there is neither craving nor dispassion.
śūnyā dṛṣṭirvṛthā ceṣṭā vikalānīndriyāṇi ca na spṛhā na viraktirvā kṣīṇasaṃsārasāgare 17-9
He is neither awake nor asleep, neither opens his eyes nor closes them. Ah, what a supreme state the free mind abides in!
na jagarti na nidrāti nonmīlati na mīlati aho paradaśā kvāpi vartate muktacetasaḥ 17-10
The free one is seen everywhere at ease, everywhere pure in heart; released from all latent desires, he shines wherever he is.
sarvatra dṛśyate svasthaḥ sarvatra vimalāśayaḥ samastavāsanā mukto muktaḥ sarvatra rājate 17-11
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, taking, speaking, walking, yet free of wanting and not wanting, the great-souled one is truly free.
paśyan śṛṇvan spṛśan jighrannaśnan gṛṇhan vadan vrajan īhitānīhitairmukto mukta eva mahāśayaḥ 17-12
He neither blames nor praises, is neither elated nor angry, neither gives nor takes. The free one has no taste for anything anywhere.
na nindati na ca stauti na hṛṣyati na kupyati na dadāti na gṛṇhāti muktaḥ sarvatra nīrasaḥ 17-13
Whether he sees a woman full of love or death drawing near, the great-souled one stays steady in mind and at ease. He is truly free.
sānurāgāṃ striyaṃ dṛṣṭvā mṛtyuṃ vā samupasthitaṃ avihvalamanāḥ svastho mukta eva mahāśayaḥ 17-14
In pleasure and pain, in man and woman, in good fortune and bad, the wise one sees no difference, for he sees everything with an equal eye.
sukhe duḥkhe nare nāryāṃ saṃpatsu ca vipatsu ca viśeṣo naiva dhīrasya sarvatra samadarśinaḥ 17-15
In one whose wandering through worldly life is over, there is no violence and no pity, no arrogance and no meekness, no amazement and no agitation.
na hiṃsā naiva kāruṇyaṃ nauddhatyaṃ na ca dīnatā nāścaryaṃ naiva ca kṣobhaḥ kṣīṇasaṃsaraṇe nare 17-16
The free one neither hates sense objects nor is greedy for them. With a mind always unattached, he takes what comes and what does not come alike.
na mukto viṣayadveṣṭā na vā viṣayalolupaḥ asaṃsaktamanā nityaṃ prāptāprāptamupāśnute 17-17
With an empty mind, as if established in complete aloneness (kaivalya), he does not even know the notions of focused and unfocused, good and bad.
samādhānāsamādhānahitāhitavikalpanāḥ śūnyacitto na jānāti kaivalyamiva saṃsthitaḥ 17-18
Without 'mine', without 'I', certain that nothing is, with every hope melted away within, he does nothing even while acting.
nirmamo nirahaṃkāro na kiṃciditi niścitaḥ antargalitasarvāśaḥ kurvannapi karoti na 17-19
One whose mind has melted away reaches a state beyond words, free of the mind's display, delusion, dreaming and dullness.
manaḥprakāśasaṃmohasvapnajāḍyavivarjitaḥ daśāṃ kāmapi saṃprāpto bhaved galitamānasaḥ 17-20
Salutations to that peaceful radiance, whose nature is bliss alone, with the dawning of whose knowledge delusion at once becomes like a dream.
aṣṭāvakra uvāca yasya bodhodaye tāvatsvapnavad bhavati bhramaḥ tasmai sukhaikarūpāya namaḥ śāntāya tejase 18-1
A person may gain every kind of wealth and win abundant pleasures, yet no one can be happy without giving up everything.
arjayitvākhilān arthān bhogānāpnoti puṣkalān na hi sarvaparityāgamantareṇa sukhī bhavet 18-2
When one's inner being is scorched by the blazing sun of the pain of duties, where is happiness without a downpour of the nectar of calm?
kartavyaduḥkhamārtaṇḍajvālādagdhāntarātmanaḥ kutaḥ praśamapīyūṣadhārāsāramṛte sukham 18-3
This world is only an imagining; in truth it is nothing. But for those who see clearly into being and non-being, their own nature never ceases to be.
bhavo'yaṃ bhāvanāmātro na kiṃcit paramarthataḥ nāstyabhāvaḥ svabhāvanāṃ bhāvābhāvavibhāvinām 18-4
The state of the Self is neither far away nor gained by narrowing down; it is already attained, free of thought, effortless, changeless and stainless.
na dūraṃ na ca saṃkocāllabdhamevātmanaḥ padaṃ nirvikalpaṃ nirāyāsaṃ nirvikāraṃ niraṃjanam 18-5
Simply by ending delusion and simply by grasping their own nature, those whose sight is unveiled live radiant and free of sorrow.
vyāmohamātraviratau svarūpādānamātrataḥ vītaśokā virājante nirāvaraṇadṛṣṭayaḥ 18-6
Knowing that everything is mere imagination and that the Self is free and eternal, why would the wise one go on practising like a child?
samastaṃ kalpanāmātramātmā muktaḥ sanātanaḥ iti vijñāya dhīro hi kimabhyasyati bālavat 18-7
Having realised that the Self is Brahman and that being and non-being are imagined, what does the desireless one need to know, or say, or do?
ātmā brahmeti niścitya bhāvābhāvau ca kalpitau niṣkāmaḥ kiṃ vijānāti kiṃ brūte ca karoti kim 18-8
Notions like 'this I am' and 'this I am not' fade away for the yogi who, certain that all is the Self, has fallen silent.
ayaṃ so'hamayaṃ nāhaṃ iti kṣīṇā vikalpanā sarvamātmeti niścitya tūṣṇīṃbhūtasya yoginaḥ 18-9
For the yogi who has become wholly calm there is no distraction and no focus, no heightened knowing and no dullness, no pleasure and no pain.
na vikṣepo na caikāgryaṃ nātibodho na mūḍhatā na sukhaṃ na ca vā duḥkhaṃ upaśāntasya yoginaḥ 18-10
Ruling a kingdom or living on alms, gain or loss, among people or in the forest: it makes no difference to the yogi whose nature is free of thought.
svārājye bhaikṣavṛttau ca lābhālābhe jane vane nirvikalpasvabhāvasya na viśeṣo'sti yoginaḥ 18-11
Where is duty, where is pleasure, where is wealth, where is discernment, for the yogi freed from opposites like 'this is done, this is not done'?
kva dharmaḥ kva ca vā kāmaḥ kva cārthaḥ kva vivekitā idaṃ kṛtamidaṃ neti dvandvairmuktasya yoginaḥ 18-12
For the yogi who is free while living, there is nothing at all left to do and no attachment in the heart; he simply lives as life comes.
kṛtyaṃ kimapi naivāsti na kāpi hṛdi raṃjanā yathā jīvanameveha jīvanmuktasya yoginaḥ 18-13
Where is delusion, where is the world, where is meditation on it, where is liberation, for the great soul who rests at the far edge of all intentions?
kva mohaḥ kva ca vā viśvaṃ kva tad dhyānaṃ kva muktatā sarvasaṃkalpasīmāyāṃ viśrāntasya mahātmanaḥ 18-14
Let the one who has seen this world try to deny it. But what is there for one without latent desires to do? Even seeing, he does not see.
yena viśvamidaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ sa nāstīti karotu vai nirvāsanaḥ kiṃ kurute paśyannapi na paśyati 18-15
One who has seen the supreme Brahman may meditate, 'I am Brahman.' But what is there to think about for one beyond thought, who sees no second?
yena dṛṣṭaṃ paraṃ brahma so'haṃ brahmeti cintayet kiṃ cintayati niścinto dvitīyaṃ yo na paśyati 18-16
One who has noticed his own distraction tries to restrain it. But the noble one is not distracted; with nothing to achieve, what should he do?
dṛṣṭo yenātmavikṣepo nirodhaṃ kurute tvasau udārastu na vikṣiptaḥ sādhyābhāvātkaroti kim 18-17
The wise one, the reverse of ordinary people, though he lives just as they do, sees in himself neither samadhi nor distraction nor any taint.
dhīro lokaviparyasto vartamāno'pi lokavat na samādhiṃ na vikṣepaṃ na lepaṃ svasya paśyati 18-18
The awakened one, beyond being and non-being, content and free of latent desire, does nothing at all, though in the world's eyes he acts.
bhāvābhāvavihīno yastṛpto nirvāsano budhaḥ naiva kiṃcitkṛtaṃ tena lokadṛṣṭyā vikurvatā 18-19
The wise one does not cling to either activity or withdrawal. Whatever comes to be done, he does it and stays at ease.
pravṛttau vā nivṛttau vā naiva dhīrasya durgrahaḥ yadā yatkartumāyāti tatkṛtvā tiṣṭhataḥ sukham 18-20
Free of latent desires, leaning on nothing, moving as he pleases, his bonds undone, he is tossed by the wind of past impressions and drifts about like a dry leaf.
nirvāsano nirālaṃbaḥ svacchando muktabandhanaḥ kṣiptaḥ saṃskāravātena ceṣṭate śuṣkaparṇavat 18-21
For one who has gone beyond samsara there is no elation and no dejection anywhere. His mind always cool, he shines as though he had no body.
asaṃsārasya tu kvāpi na harṣo na viṣāditā sa śītalamanā nityaṃ videha iva rājate 18-22
The wise one who delights in the Self, whose inner being is cool and clear, has no wish to give anything up and no sense of loss, anywhere.
kutrāpi na jihāsāsti nāśo vāpi na kutracit ātmārāmasya dhīrasya śītalācchatarātmanaḥ 18-23
His mind empty by nature, acting on whatever comes, the wise one may look like an ordinary person, yet he knows neither pride nor humiliation.
prakṛtyā śūnyacittasya kurvato'sya yadṛcchayā prākṛtasyeva dhīrasya na māno nāvamānatā 18-24
"This action was done by the body, not by me, who am pure by nature." One who keeps to this understanding does nothing, even while acting.
kṛtaṃ dehena karmedaṃ na mayā śuddharūpiṇā iti cintānurodhī yaḥ kurvannapi karoti na 18-25
He acts like one who does not profess this teaching, yet he is no simpleton. Free while living, happy and graced, he shines even as he moves through the world.
atadvādīva kurute na bhavedapi bāliśaḥ jīvanmuktaḥ sukhī śrīmān saṃsarannapi śobhate 18-26
Worn out by endless reasoning, the wise one has come to rest. He no longer imagines, knows, hears or sees.
nānāvicārasuśrānto dhīro viśrāntimāgataḥ na kalpate na jānāti na śṛṇoti na paśyati 18-27
Since he is neither in samadhi nor distracted, he is neither a seeker of liberation nor its opposite. Seeing with certainty that all this is imagined, the great-souled one simply remains as Brahman.
asamādheravikṣepān na mumukṣurna cetaraḥ niścitya kalpitaṃ paśyan brahmaivāste mahāśayaḥ 18-28
One who carries ego within is acting even when he does nothing. For the wise one free of ego, nothing is done and nothing is left undone.
yasyāntaḥ syādahaṃkāro na karoti karoti saḥ nirahaṃkāradhīreṇa na kiṃcidakṛtaṃ kṛtam 18-29
The mind of the free one shines: not agitated and not gratified, not acting, without stirring, without hopes, its doubts gone.
nodvignaṃ na ca santuṣṭamakartṛ spandavarjitaṃ nirāśaṃ gatasandehaṃ cittaṃ muktasya rājate 18-30
The free one's mind does not set out to meditate or to act; yet, without any reason, it meditates and it acts.
nirdhyātuṃ ceṣṭituṃ vāpi yaccittaṃ na pravartate nirnimittamidaṃ kiṃtu nirdhyāyati viceṣṭate 18-31
Hearing the truth as it really is, a dull person becomes bewildered; while some who are not deluded draw inward and seem like fools.
tattvaṃ yathārthamākarṇya mandaḥ prāpnoti mūḍhatāṃ athavā yāti saṃkocamamūḍhaḥ ko'pi mūḍhavat 18-32
The deluded labour hard at concentration and at stilling the mind. The wise, resting in their own state as if asleep, see nothing that needs to be done.
ekāgratā nirodho vā mūḍhairabhyasyate bhṛśaṃ dhīrāḥ kṛtyaṃ na paśyanti suptavatsvapade sthitāḥ 18-33
Neither by effort nor by giving up effort does the deluded one find peace. The wise one is at peace simply by being certain of the truth.
aprayatnāt prayatnād vā mūḍho nāpnoti nirvṛtiṃ tattvaniścayamātreṇa prājño bhavati nirvṛtaḥ 18-34
The Self is pure, awake, beloved, complete, beyond the world's spread and free of all ill. People absorbed in practice do not know it.
śuddhaṃ buddhaṃ priyaṃ pūrṇaṃ niṣprapaṃcaṃ nirāmayaṃ ātmānaṃ taṃ na jānanti tatrābhyāsaparā janāḥ 18-35
The deluded one does not reach liberation through the action of repeated practice. The blessed one, through understanding alone, is free and remains unchanged.
nāpnoti karmaṇā mokṣaṃ vimūḍho'bhyāsarūpiṇā dhanyo vijñānamātreṇa muktastiṣṭhatyavikriyaḥ 18-36
The deluded one does not reach Brahman, because he wants to become it. The wise one, without even wanting it, already shares the nature of the supreme Brahman.
mūḍho nāpnoti tad brahma yato bhavitumicchati anicchannapi dhīro hi parabrahmasvarūpabhāk 18-37
Without real ground and restless to grasp, the deluded keep feeding samsara. The wise have cut this root of all misery at its root.
nirādhārā grahavyagrā mūḍhāḥ saṃsārapoṣakāḥ etasyānarthamūlasya mūlacchedaḥ kṛto budhaiḥ 18-38
The deluded one finds no peace, because he tries to make himself peaceful. The wise one, having settled the truth, is at peace in mind always.
na śāntiṃ labhate mūḍho yataḥ śamitumicchati dhīrastattvaṃ viniścitya sarvadā śāntamānasaḥ 18-39
How can one who leans on what is seen ever see the Self? The wise do not see this or that; they see the imperishable Self.
kvātmano darśanaṃ tasya yad dṛṣṭamavalaṃbate dhīrāstaṃ taṃ na paśyanti paśyantyātmānamavyayam 18-40
Where is stillness for the deluded one, who forces his mind? For the wise one who delights in himself, it is always natural.
kva nirodho vimūḍhasya yo nirbandhaṃ karoti vai svārāmasyaiva dhīrasya sarvadāsāvakṛtrimaḥ 18-41
One person holds that things exist, another holds that nothing exists. Rare is the one who holds to neither; he alone is at ease.
bhāvasya bhāvakaḥ kaścin na kiṃcid bhāvakoparaḥ ubhayābhāvakaḥ kaścid evameva nirākulaḥ 18-42
People of poor understanding meditate on the Self as pure and non-dual, but in their confusion they never actually know it, and remain unfulfilled all their lives.
śuddhamadvayamātmānaṃ bhāvayanti kubuddhayaḥ na tu jānanti saṃmohādyāvajjīvamanirvṛtāḥ 18-43
The mind of one seeking liberation cannot stand without something to lean on. The mind of the free one is always without support and without desire.
mumukṣorbuddhirālaṃbamantareṇa na vidyate nirālaṃbaiva niṣkāmā buddhirmuktasya sarvadā 18-44
Seeing the tigers of sense-objects, the frightened run for refuge and quickly crawl into a cave, hoping to achieve control and concentration of mind.
viṣayadvīpino vīkṣya cakitāḥ śaraṇārthinaḥ viśanti jhaṭiti kroḍaṃ nirodhaikāgrasiddhaye 18-45
Seeing the lion who is free of craving, the elephants of sense-objects quietly flee; those that cannot, stay and serve him like flatterers.
nirvāsanaṃ hariṃ dṛṣṭvā tūṣṇīṃ viṣayadantinaḥ palāyante na śaktāste sevante kṛtacāṭavaḥ 18-46
Free of doubt and with a settled mind, he takes up no methods for liberation. Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, he lives at ease.
na muktikārikāṃ dhatte niḥśaṅko yuktamānasaḥ paśyan śṛṇvan spṛśan jighrannaśnannāste yathāsukham 18-47
Just by hearing the truth, his mind becomes pure and untroubled. He sees no proper conduct, no improper conduct, and no indifference either.
vastuśravaṇamātreṇa śuddhabuddhirnirākulaḥ naivācāramanācāramaudāsyaṃ vā prapaśyati 18-48
Whatever comes to be done, the simple one does it then and there, good or bad; his actions are like a child's.
yadā yatkartumāyāti tadā tatkurute ṛjuḥ śubhaṃ vāpyaśubhaṃ vāpi tasya ceṣṭā hi bālavat 18-49
Through freedom one finds happiness; through freedom one gains the highest; through freedom one reaches peace; through freedom, the supreme state.
svātaṃtryātsukhamāpnoti svātaṃtryāllabhate paraṃ svātaṃtryānnirvṛtiṃ gacchetsvātaṃtryāt paramaṃ padam 18-50
When one recognises one's own Self as neither the doer nor the enjoyer, all the movements of the mind simply wear away.
akartṛtvamabhoktṛtvaṃ svātmano manyate yadā tadā kṣīṇā bhavantyeva samastāścittavṛttayaḥ 18-51
The wise one's way of being shines, unrestrained and unplanned though it is; not so the forced calm of the deluded one whose mind is full of craving.
ucchṛṃkhalāpyakṛtikā sthitirdhīrasya rājate na tu saspṛhacittasya śāntirmūḍhasya kṛtrimā 18-52
The wise, free of imaginings, unbound, their minds free, may enjoy great luxuries or retreat into mountain caves.
vilasanti mahābhogairviśanti girigahvarān nirastakalpanā dhīrā abaddhā muktabuddhayaḥ 18-53
Seeing and honouring a learned Vedic priest, a deity, a holy place, a woman, a king or a loved one, the wise one feels no craving in his heart.
śrotriyaṃ devatāṃ tīrthamaṅganāṃ bhūpatiṃ priyaṃ dṛṣṭvā saṃpūjya dhīrasya na kāpi hṛdi vāsanā 18-54
Even when servants, sons, wives, grandsons and relatives laugh at him and scorn him, the yogi is not disturbed in the least.
bhṛtyaiḥ putraiḥ kalatraiśca dauhitraiścāpi gotrajaiḥ vihasya dhikkṛto yogī na yāti vikṛtiṃ manāk 18-55
Pleased, he is not pleased; pained, he does not suffer. Only those like him understand that wondrous state of his.
santuṣṭo'pi na santuṣṭaḥ khinno'pi na ca khidyate tasyāścaryadaśāṃ tāṃ tāṃ tādṛśā eva jānate 18-56
The feeling that something must be done is itself samsara. The wise do not see it, for their very form is emptiness: formless, unchanging and untouched by ill.
kartavyataiva saṃsāro na tāṃ paśyanti sūrayaḥ śūnyākārā nirākārā nirvikārā nirāmayāḥ 18-57
The deluded one is anxious and restless everywhere, even when doing nothing. The capable one stays untroubled, even while doing what has to be done.
akurvannapi saṃkṣobhād vyagraḥ sarvatra mūḍhadhīḥ kurvannapi tu kṛtyāni kuśalo hi nirākulaḥ 18-58
Happily he sits, happily he sleeps, happily he comes and goes, happily he speaks, happily he eats: the one whose mind is at peace, even in everyday life.
sukhamāste sukhaṃ śete sukhamāyāti yāti ca sukhaṃ vakti sukhaṃ bhuṃkte vyavahāre'pi śāntadhīḥ 18-59
By his very nature he feels no distress, though he deals with the world like anyone else. Calm as a vast lake, his troubles gone, he shines.
svabhāvādyasya naivārtirlokavad vyavahāriṇaḥ mahāhṛda ivākṣobhyo gatakleśaḥ sa śobhate 18-60
For the deluded one, even withdrawing from action turns into activity. For the wise one, even activity bears the fruit of withdrawal.
nivṛttirapi mūḍhasya pravṛtti rupajāyate pravṛttirapi dhīrasya nivṛttiphalabhāginī 18-61
The deluded one often shows distaste for possessions. But for one whose attachment even to the body has fallen away, where is liking and where is distaste?
parigraheṣu vairāgyaṃ prāyo mūḍhasya dṛśyate dehe vigalitāśasya kva rāgaḥ kva virāgatā 18-62
The deluded one's outlook always clings to contemplating or not contemplating. The settled one, though he contemplates what comes, has an outlook that is no outlook at all.
bhāvanābhāvanāsaktā dṛṣṭirmūḍhasya sarvadā bhāvyabhāvanayā sā tu svasthasyādṛṣṭirūpiṇī 18-63
The sage who goes about all undertakings without desire, like a child, is pure; no action clings to him, even as it is being done.
sarvāraṃbheṣu niṣkāmo yaścared bālavan muniḥ na lepastasya śuddhasya kriyamāṇe'pi karmaṇi 18-64
Blessed indeed is the knower of the Self who is the same toward all things; seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, his mind is free of thirst.
sa eva dhanya ātmajñaḥ sarvabhāveṣu yaḥ samaḥ paśyan śṛṇvan spṛśan jighrann aśnannistarṣamānasaḥ 18-65
For the wise one who is always free of mental constructs, like the sky, where is samsara, where is appearance, where is a goal, where a means?
kva saṃsāraḥ kva cābhāsaḥ kva sādhyaṃ kva ca sādhanaṃ ākāśasyeva dhīrasya nirvikalpasya sarvadā 18-66
Victory to the one who has renounced all aims, whose very form is the fullness of his own bliss, whose natural samadhi abides in the boundless.
sa jayatyarthasaṃnyāsī pūrṇasvarasavigrahaḥ akṛtrimo'navacchinne samādhiryasya vartate 18-67
Why say more? The great-souled one who has known the truth wants neither enjoyment nor liberation, and finds no relish in anything, always and everywhere.
bahunātra kimuktena jñātatattvo mahāśayaḥ bhogamokṣanirākāṃkṣī sadā sarvatra nīrasaḥ 18-68
The dual world, from mahat onward, is just an unfolding of names. Once that is let go, what is left to do for one who is pure awareness?
mahadādi jagaddvaitaṃ nāmamātravijṛṃbhitaṃ vihāya śuddhabodhasya kiṃ kṛtyamavaśiṣyate 18-69
Certain that all this is a product of illusion and that nothing truly is, the pure one, whose light cannot be made an object, comes to rest by his very nature.
bhramabhūtamidaṃ sarvaṃ kiṃcinnāstīti niścayī alakṣyasphuraṇaḥ śuddhaḥ svabhāvenaiva śāmyati 18-70
For one whose nature is pure radiance and who sees no world of objects, where is rule, where dispassion, where renunciation, where even calm?
śuddhasphuraṇarūpasya dṛśyabhāvamapaśyataḥ kva vidhiḥ kva ca vairāgyaṃ kva tyāgaḥ kva śamo'pi vā 18-71
For one who shines as the infinite and does not see nature at all, where is bondage, where liberation, where joy, where sorrow?
sphurato'nantarūpeṇa prakṛtiṃ ca na paśyataḥ kva bandhaḥ kva ca vā mokṣaḥ kva harṣaḥ kva viṣāditā 18-72
In a samsara that reaches only as far as the intellect, mere illusion plays itself out. The wise one, free of 'mine', free of ego and free of desire, shines.
buddhiparyantasaṃsāre māyāmātraṃ vivartate nirmamo nirahaṃkāro niṣkāmaḥ śobhate budhaḥ 18-73
For the sage who sees the Self as imperishable and free of sorrow, where is knowledge, where is the world, where the thought 'I am the body' or 'this is mine'?
akṣayaṃ gatasantāpamātmānaṃ paśyato muneḥ kva vidyā ca kva vā viśvaṃ kva deho'haṃ mameti vā 18-74
If a dull-minded person gives up practices such as stilling the mind, he falls at once into daydreams and idle chatter.
nirodhādīni karmāṇi jahāti jaḍadhīryadi manorathān pralāpāṃśca kartumāpnotyatatkṣaṇāt 18-75
The dull one, even after hearing that truth, does not give up his delusion. Outwardly he strains to be free of thought, but inwardly he hungers for objects.
mandaḥ śrutvāpi tadvastu na jahāti vimūḍhatāṃ nirvikalpo bahiryatnādantarviṣayalālasaḥ 18-76
One whose actions have fallen away through knowledge, though in the world's eyes he still acts, finds no occasion to do or to say anything at all.
jñānād galitakarmā yo lokadṛṣṭyāpi karmakṛt nāpnotyavasaraṃ kartuṃ vaktumeva na kiṃcana 18-77
For the wise one who is always unchanging and without fear, where is darkness, where light, where renunciation? There is nothing at all.
kva tamaḥ kva prakāśo vā hānaṃ kva ca na kiṃcana nirvikārasya dhīrasya nirātaṃkasya sarvadā 18-78
For the yogi whose nature cannot be put into words, who has no fixed nature at all, where is steadiness, where discernment, where even fearlessness?
kva dhairyaṃ kva vivekitvaṃ kva nirātaṃkatāpi vā anirvācyasvabhāvasya niḥsvabhāvasya yoginaḥ 18-79
There is no heaven, no hell, not even liberation while living. In short, in the yogi's vision there is nothing at all.
na svargo naiva narako jīvanmuktirna caiva hi bahunātra kimuktena yogadṛṣṭyā na kiṃcana 18-80
He neither prays for gain nor grieves over loss. The cool mind of the wise one is filled as if with nectar.
naiva prārthayate lābhaṃ nālābhenānuśocati dhīrasya śītalaṃ cittamamṛtenaiva pūritam 18-81
Free of desire, he neither praises the peaceful nor blames the wicked. Content, the same in sorrow and joy, he sees nothing that must be done.
na śāntaṃ stauti niṣkāmo na duṣṭamapi nindati samaduḥkhasukhastṛptaḥ kiṃcit kṛtyaṃ na paśyati 18-82
The wise one does not hate samsara, nor does he long to see the Self. Free of joy and anger, he is neither dead nor alive.
dhīro na dveṣṭi saṃsāramātmānaṃ na didṛkṣati harṣāmarṣavinirmukto na mṛto na ca jīvati 18-83
Without attachment to son, wife and the rest, without desire for sense-objects, unconcerned even about his own body, free of hopes, the wise one shines.
niḥsnehaḥ putradārādau niṣkāmo viṣayeṣu ca niścintaḥ svaśarīre'pi nirāśaḥ śobhate budhaḥ 18-84
The wise one is content everywhere, living on whatever comes his way, wandering freely from place to place, lying down wherever the sun sets.
tuṣṭiḥ sarvatra dhīrasya yathāpatitavartinaḥ svacchandaṃ carato deśān yatrāstamitaśāyinaḥ 18-85
Let the body fall or rise; the great soul does not care, for resting on the ground of his own nature he has forgotten all of samsara.
patatūdetu vā deho nāsya cintā mahātmanaḥ svabhāvabhūmiviśrāntivismṛtāśeṣasaṃsṛteḥ 18-86
Owning nothing, moving as he pleases, beyond the pairs of opposites, his doubts cut away, unattached to all things, the wise one delights, alone.
akiṃcanaḥ kāmacāro nirdvandvaśchinnasaṃśayaḥ asaktaḥ sarvabhāveṣu kevalo ramate budhaḥ 18-87
The wise one, free of 'mine', shines; to him a clod of earth, a stone and gold are all the same. The knot of his heart is cut through, and restlessness and dullness are shaken off.
nirmamaḥ śobhate dhīraḥ samaloṣṭāśmakāṃcanaḥ subhinnahṛdayagranthirvinirdhūtarajastamaḥ 18-88
He fixes his attention on nothing in particular, and no craving remains in his heart. With whom could such a free and fully content soul be compared?
sarvatrānavadhānasya na kiṃcid vāsanā hṛdi muktātmano vitṛptasya tulanā kena jāyate 18-89
Knowing, he does not know; seeing, he does not see; speaking, he does not speak. Who could this be but one free of all craving?
jānannapi na jānāti paśyannapi na paśyati bruvann api na ca brūte ko'nyo nirvāsanādṛte 18-90
Beggar or king, the one who is free of desire shines, the one whose sense of things as good or bad has fallen away.
bhikṣurvā bhūpatirvāpi yo niṣkāmaḥ sa śobhate bhāveṣu galitā yasya śobhanāśobhanā matiḥ 18-91
For the yogi who has become simple and without guile, whose purpose is fulfilled, where is license, where restraint, where even the settling of truth?
kva svācchandyaṃ kva saṃkocaḥ kva vā tattvaviniścayaḥ nirvyājārjavabhūtasya caritārthasya yoginaḥ 18-92
What is felt within by one content in resting in the Self, free of hope and free of pain — how could it be told, and to whom?
ātmaviśrāntitṛptena nirāśena gatārtinā antaryadanubhūyeta tat kathaṃ kasya kathyate 18-93
Asleep, he is not in deep sleep; in dream, he is not asleep; awake, he is not awake. The wise one is content at every step.
supto'pi na suṣuptau ca svapne'pi śayito na ca jāgare'pi na jāgarti dhīrastṛptaḥ pade pade 18-94
The knower, though he has thoughts, is free of thought; though he has senses, is beyond the senses; though he has intellect, is beyond intellect; though he has an ego, is without ego.
jñaḥ sacinto'pi niścintaḥ sendriyo'pi nirindriyaḥ sabuddhirapi nirbuddhiḥ sāhaṃkāro'nahaṅkṛtiḥ 18-95
He is neither happy nor sad, neither detached nor attached, neither seeking liberation nor liberated; he is neither something nor nothing.
na sukhī na ca vā duḥkhī na virakto na saṃgavān na mumukṣurna vā mukto na kiṃcinna ca kiṃcana 18-96
The blessed one is not distracted in distraction, not absorbed in samadhi, not dull in dullness, and not learned in learning.
vikṣepe'pi na vikṣiptaḥ samādhau na samādhimān jāḍye'pi na jaḍo dhanyaḥ pāṇḍitye'pi na paṇḍitaḥ 18-97
The free one, at ease with things as they are, at peace having done what was to be done, the same everywhere, free of thirst, does not dwell on what he did or left undone.
mukto yathāsthitisvasthaḥ kṛtakartavyanirvṛtaḥ samaḥ sarvatra vaitṛṣṇyānna smaratyakṛtaṃ kṛtam 18-98
He is not pleased when praised, nor angered when blamed. He neither dreads death nor rejoices in life.
na prīyate vandyamāno nindyamāno na kupyati naivodvijati maraṇe jīvane nābhinandati 18-99
The one whose mind is at peace runs neither toward the crowd nor toward the forest. However things are, wherever he is, he remains the same.
na dhāvati janākīrṇaṃ nāraṇyaṃ upaśāntadhīḥ yathātathā yatratatra sama evāvatiṣṭhate 18-100
With the tongs of the knowledge of truth, I have pulled out from deep within my heart the thorn of countless opinions.
janaka uvāca tattvavijñānasandaṃśamādāya hṛdayodarāt nānāvidhaparāmarśaśalyoddhāraḥ kṛto mayā 19-1
Where is duty, where is pleasure, where is wealth, where is discernment? Where is duality, and where is non-duality, for me who abides in my own glory?
kva dharmaḥ kva ca vā kāmaḥ kva cārthaḥ kva vivekitā kva dvaitaṃ kva ca vā'dvaitaṃ svamahimni sthitasya me 19-2
Where is the past, where is the future, where even the present? Where is space, and where is eternity, for me who abides in my own glory?
kva bhūtaṃ kva bhaviṣyad vā vartamānamapi kva vā kva deśaḥ kva ca vā nityaṃ svamahimni sthitasya me 19-3
Where is the Self, where is the not-Self, where is good, where is bad? Where is thought, and where is no-thought, for me who abides in my own glory?
kva cātmā kva ca vānātmā kva śubhaṃ kvāśubhaṃ yathā kva cintā kva ca vācintā svamahimni sthitasya me 19-4
Where is dreaming, where is deep sleep, where is waking? Where is the fourth state, or even fear, for me who abides in my own glory?
kva svapnaḥ kva suṣuptirvā kva ca jāgaraṇaṃ tathā kva turiyaṃ bhayaṃ vāpi svamahimni sthitasya me 19-5
Where is far, where is near, where is outside, where is inside? Where is gross, and where is subtle, for me who abides in my own glory?
kva dūraṃ kva samīpaṃ vā bāhyaṃ kvābhyantaraṃ kva vā kva sthūlaṃ kva ca vā sūkṣmaṃ svamahimni sthitasya me 19-6
Where is death, where is life, where are the worlds, and where are worldly affairs? Where is dissolution, and where is samadhi, for me who abides in my own glory?
kva mṛtyurjīvitaṃ vā kva lokāḥ kvāsya kva laukikaṃ kva layaḥ kva samādhirvā svamahimni sthitasya me 19-7
Enough of talk about the three aims of life, enough of talk about yoga, enough even of talk about knowledge, for me who rests in the Self.
alaṃ trivargakathayā yogasya kathayāpyalaṃ alaṃ vijñānakathayā viśrāntasya mamātmani 19-8
Where are the elements, where is the body, where are the senses, where is the mind? Where is emptiness, and where is despair, in my own stainless nature?
janaka uvāca kva bhūtāni kva deho vā kvendriyāṇi kva vā manaḥ kva śūnyaṃ kva ca nairāśyaṃ matsvarūpe niraṃjane 20-1
Where is scripture, where is knowledge of the Self, where is a mind free of objects? Where is contentment, and where is freedom from craving, for me who am always beyond the pairs of opposites?
kva śāstraṃ kvātmavijñānaṃ kva vā nirviṣayaṃ manaḥ kva tṛptiḥ kva vitṛṣṇātvaṃ gatadvandvasya me sadā 20-2
Where is knowledge, where is ignorance, where is 'I', where is 'this', where is 'mine'? Where is bondage, where is liberation? How can my own nature have any form?
kva vidyā kva ca vāvidyā kvāhaṃ kvedaṃ mama kva vā kva bandhaḥ kva ca vā mokṣaḥ svarūpasya kva rūpitā 20-3
Where are the past actions now bearing fruit, where is liberation while living, and where is that final freedom after the body falls, for me who am always without distinctions?
kva prārabdhāni karmāṇi jīvanmuktirapi kva vā kva tad videhakaivalyaṃ nirviśeṣasya sarvadā 20-4
Where is the doer, where is the enjoyer, where is actionless shining? Where is direct realisation, and where is its fruit, for me who am always without any nature of my own?
kva kartā kva ca vā bhoktā niṣkriyaṃ sphuraṇaṃ kva vā kvāparokṣaṃ phalaṃ vā kva niḥsvabhāvasya me sadā 20-5
Where is the world, where is the seeker of liberation, where is the yogi, where is the knower? Where is the bound, and where is the free, for me in my own non-dual nature?
kva lokaḥ kva mumukṣurvā kva yogī jñānavān kva vā kva baddhaḥ kva ca vā muktaḥ svasvarūpe'hamadvaye 20-6
Where is creation, where is destruction, where is the goal, where is the means? Where is the seeker, and where is attainment, for me in my own non-dual nature?
kva sṛṣṭiḥ kva ca saṃhāraḥ kva sādhyaṃ kva ca sādhanaṃ kva sādhakaḥ kva siddhirvā svasvarūpe'hamadvaye 20-7
Where is the knower, where is the means of knowing, where is the known, where is knowing itself? Where is something, and where is nothing, for me who am always pure?
kva pramātā pramāṇaṃ vā kva prameyaṃ kva ca pramā kva kiṃcit kva na kiṃcid vā sarvadā vimalasya me 20-8
Where is distraction, where is one-pointedness, where is dullness, where is delusion? Where is joy, and where is sorrow, for me who am always actionless?
kva vikṣepaḥ kva caikāgryaṃ kva nirbodhaḥ kva mūḍhatā kva harṣaḥ kva viṣādo vā sarvadā niṣkriyasya me 20-9
Where is everyday life, and where is ultimate truth? Where is happiness, and where is sorrow, for me who am always beyond thought?
kva caiṣa vyavahāro vā kva ca sā paramārthatā kva sukhaṃ kva ca vā dukhaṃ nirvimarśasya me sadā 20-10
Where is illusion, where is worldly life, where is attachment, where is detachment? Where is the individual soul, and where is that Brahman, for me who am always pure?
kva māyā kva ca saṃsāraḥ kva prītirviratiḥ kva vā kva jīvaḥ kva ca tadbrahma sarvadā vimalasya me 20-11
Where is activity, where is withdrawal, where is liberation, where is bondage, for me who am always unchanging, undivided and at rest in myself?
kva pravṛttirnirvṛttirvā kva muktiḥ kva ca bandhanaṃ kūṭasthanirvibhāgasya svasthasya mama sarvadā 20-12
Where is instruction, where is scripture, where is the disciple, where is the teacher? Where is any goal of life, for me who am free of all limits and auspicious?
kvopadeśaḥ kva vā śāstraṃ kva śiṣyaḥ kva ca vā guruḥ kva cāsti puruṣārtho vā nirupādheḥ śivasya me 20-13
Where is existence, where is non-existence, where is oneness, where is twoness? What more is there to say? Nothing at all arises for me.
kva cāsti kva ca vā nāsti kvāsti caikaṃ kva ca dvayaṃ bahunātra kimuktena kiṃcinnottiṣṭhate mama 20-14

Three kinds of students, one teacher, one syllable, and three different lessons.

Death shows a boy a chariot, wild horses, and a rider who is none of them.
Alone with a herd for years, a young man learns from a bull, fire and birds.

A teacher's parting words to a student about to go out into the world.
A scholar comes to teach a king, runs out of answers, and learns from a sleeper.

Twelve years of service, no teaching, a heartsick student. Then the fires start to speak.
A starving scholar eats a stranger's leftovers, then halts the singing at a king's sacrifice.

Two short lines that tell you how to hold everything you own.

Three lines murmured during an ancient chant, and the Upanishad's own key to what they mean.

Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowing
A wealthy householder asks for the one thing that makes everything else make sense.
